hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 undergoes increased aggregation in the endo-lysosome compared with APOE3.
A: APOE genotype or apoE isoform (APOE4 vs APOE3)
B: aggregation of apoE protein itself in the endosome/lysosome (endo-lysosomal apoE aggregates, oligomers)
scope: IN: aggregation, oligomerization, misfolding or insoluble/high-molecular-weight apoE itself, especially inside endosomes/lysosomes or at acidic pH (in cells, tissue or in vitro), compared between apoE4 and apoE3; lysosomal accumulation or impaired degradation of apoE protein; apoE aggregates seeding other proteins when apoE aggregation itself is measured. OUT: amyloid-beta or tau aggregation without measuring apoE aggregation, general lysosomal function without apoE protein readouts.

rows.Finding description: At pH 4.5, PUFA-CE–lipidated ApoE4 formed more sedimentable aggregates than ApoE3 after four days at 37°C in a cell-free assay.
rows.Finding quote: Interestingly, CE(20:4)-ApoE3 demonstrated the lowest aggregation at both pH 7.4 and pH 4.5, while CE(20:4)-ApoE2 exhibited the highest aggregation at pH 7.4 but comparable aggregation as CE(20:4)-ApoE4 at pH 4.5 (Figure 5O–Q, Figure S5K).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (higher ApoE aggregation at lysosomal pH)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free HEK293-derived human ApoE lipidated with POPC and CE(20:4); 0.5 mg/mL protein in PBS adjusted to pH 4.5, four days at 37°C; ultracentrifugation at 150,000 × g for 30 minutes and non-reducing SDS-PAGE of supernatant and pellet.

rows.Finding description: Quantification across two PUFA-CE–ApoE preparation batches showed greater acidic-pH ApoE aggregation for ApoE4 than ApoE3, with variable absolute aggregation between batches.
rows.Finding quote: Interestingly, CE(20:4)-ApoE3 demonstrated the lowest aggregation at both pH 7.4 and pH 4.5, while CE(20:4)-ApoE2 exhibited the highest aggregation at pH 7.4 but comparable aggregation as CE(20:4)-ApoE4 at pH 4.5 (Figure 5O–Q, Figure S5K). Despite variability in the extent of aggregation across two independent batches of lipidated ApoE, the pH- and ApoE isoform-dependent aggregation of CE(20:4)-lipApoE was conserved.
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (higher pelletable ApoE at lysosomal pH across preparation batches)
rows.Experimental system: Two independently prepared batches of HEK293-derived human CE(20:4)/POPC-lipidated ApoE; four-day incubation at 37°C and pH 4.5; ultracentrifugation followed by densitometry of the 34 kDa ApoE band.

rows.Finding description: Human APOE-knockout iPSC astrocytes internalized more ApoE4 than ApoE3 after one day of lipidated ApoE treatment; the Manders coefficient for LAMP1-positive vesicles containing ApoE was 0.497 for ApoE4 versus 0.410 for ApoE3.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE isoform differences were manifested in the differential levels of internalized lipApoE (ApoE4 > ApoE3 > ApoE2), giving rise to the same isoform trend for LAMP1-positive vesicles containing ApoE immunoreactivity (Mander’s coefficients = 0.266 ± 0.045 for ApoE2, 0.410 ± 0.049 for ApoE3, 0.497 ± 0.090 for ApoE4) (Figure 2I).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (higher intracellular ApoE protein accumulation)
rows.Experimental system: Human APOE-knockout iPSC-derived astrocytes from ThermoFisher A18945; one-day treatment with 10 μg/mL HEK293-derived POPC-lipidated human ApoE; fixed-cell ApoE immunofluorescence with super-resolution imaging.

rows.Finding description: Internalized ApoE colocalized completely with LDLR for all three isoforms. ApoE–LAMP1 coefficients were similar for ApoE3 (0.903 ± 0.024) and ApoE4 (0.900 ± 0.008).
rows.Finding quote: Super-resolution imaging on APOE KO iAstrocytes confirmed internalized lipApoE completely colocalized with endogenous LDLR (Mander’s coefficient for ApoE puncta with colocalizing LDLR = 1 for all 3 isoforms), largely inside LAMP1 compartments (Figure 2H) (Mander’s coefficients for ApoE puncta with colocalizing LAMP1 = 0.823 ± 0.061 for ApoE2; 0.903 ± 0.024 for ApoE3; 0.900 ± 0.008 for ApoE4).
rows.Finding summary: (lipidated ApoE4 exposure) -> (predominantly lysosomal localization of internalized ApoE4)
rows.Experimental system: Human APOE-knockout iPSC-derived astrocytes generated from ThermoFisher A18945, originally APOE3/3; one-day treatment with 10 μg/mL POPC-lipidated ApoE4; ApoE, LDLR and LAMP1 immunostaining, Leica SP8 super-resolution imaging, ImageJ Coloc2.

rows.Finding description: At pH 7.4, PUFA-CE–lipidated ApoE3 showed less aggregation than ApoE4 after four days at 37°C, although the preparations remained largely soluble.
rows.Finding quote: CE(20:4)-lipApoE remained largely soluble and mostly recovered in the supernatant fraction upon incubation at pH 7.4, but abundant protein was found in the pellet fraction indicative of aggregation after incubation at pH 4.5, which mimics lysosomal pH (Figure 5O–P). Interestingly, CE(20:4)-ApoE3 demonstrated the lowest aggregation at both pH 7.4 and pH 4.5, while CE(20:4)-ApoE2 exhibited the highest aggregation at pH 7.4 but comparable aggregation as CE(20:4)-ApoE4 at pH 4.5 (Figure 5O–Q, Figure S5K).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (higher ApoE aggregation at neutral pH)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free HEK293-derived human ApoE3 or ApoE4 lipidated with POPC and CE(20:4); 0.5 mg/mL protein in PBS, pH 7.4, four days at 37°C; ultracentrifugation and non-reducing SDS-PAGE.

rows.Finding description: At pH 4.0, three-state modeling placed the maximum intermediate population at 3.75 M urea for apoE4, approximately 90%, versus 4.75 M for apoE3, approximately 80%, indicating that apoE4 formed the intermediate under milder denaturation.
rows.Finding quote: The concentration of urea at which the folding intermediate was at maximum concentration was 3.75 M for the apoE4 22- kDa fragment (90%) and 4.75 M for the apoE3 fragment (80%).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower urea concentration for maximal intermediate formation and higher maximal intermediate fraction)
rows.Experimental system: Model-derived equilibrium populations of native, intermediate, and unfolded states for recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 22-kDa amino-terminal fragments at pH 4.0; derived from circular-dichroism urea-denaturation curves; maxima occur at different urea concentrations.

rows.Finding description: At pH 4.0 in 3.75 M urea, apoE4 underwent more extensive pepsin cleavage than apoE3 despite producing the same fragment bands, consistent with greater apoE4 conformational exposure.
rows.Finding quote: Digestion of the apoE3 22-kDa fragment in 3.75 M urea yielded the same bands as the apoE4 digestion but with less proteolysis of the intact apoE3 fragment (Fig. 3, middle panels).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (greater proteolytic susceptibility at pH 4.0 in 3.75 M urea)
rows.Experimental system: Recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 22-kDa amino-terminal fragments, 0.1 mg/ml, at pH 4.0 in 3.75 M urea; room-temperature limited pepsin digestion at a 250:1 apoE:pepsin mass ratio; SDS-PAGE and amino-terminal sequencing; apoE4 digestion yielded seven major bands.

rows.Finding description: At pH 4.0, apoE4 unfolded more readily than apoE3, while both isoforms displayed plateaus consistent with stable partially unfolded intermediates.
rows.Finding quote: At pH 7.4, apoE3 and apoE4 reflected an apparent two-state denaturation. The midpoints of denaturation were 5.2 and 4.3 M urea, respectively. At pH 4.0, a pH value known to stabilize folding intermediates, apoE4 and apoE3 dis- played the same order of denaturation but with distinct plateaus, suggesting the presence of a stable folding intermediate
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (greater susceptibility to acidic-pH unfolding, with stable intermediates in both)
rows.Experimental system: Bacterially expressed recombinant human apoE2, apoE3, and apoE4 22-kDa amino-terminal fragments; overnight urea equilibration at 4 °C in sodium acetate buffer, pH 4.0; circular dichroism at 220 nm measured at 25 °C under reducing conditions; relevant comparison is apoE4 versus apoE3.

rows.Finding description: Without urea at pH 4.0, apoE3 and apoE4 produced the same major RQQTE-starting pepsin fragment and resisted further cleavage, with no significant difference reported and no statistical test provided.
rows.Finding quote: In 0 M urea, there was one major frag- ment, which had the amino-terminal sequence of RQQTE, which corresponds to amino acids 15–19 in apoE (Fig. 3, top panels). This sequence is at the flexible amino terminus of the 22-kDa fragment that is not resolved in the x-ray structure (34). Further addition of pepsin or longer digestion times did not produce smaller cleavage products under these conditions
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (no change in the reported pepsin-cleavage pattern without urea at pH 4.0)
rows.Experimental system: Recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 22-kDa amino-terminal fragments, 0.1 mg/ml, at pH 4.0 without urea; room-temperature limited pepsin digestion at a 10:1 apoE:pepsin mass ratio; SDS-PAGE and amino-terminal sequencing.

rows.Finding description: At pH 4.0 in 4.75 M urea, apoE3 and apoE4 showed similar cleavage bands and a smaller difference in digestion extent than at 3.75 M, indicating convergence of their conformational susceptibility.
rows.Finding quote: The bands after digestion of apoE3 and apoE4 in 4.75 M urea were similar to those obtained after digestion in 3.75 M urea, but there was less difference in the extent of digestion (Fig. 3, bottom panels).
rows.Finding summary: (3.75 M -> 4.75 M urea) -> (smaller APOE4–APOE3 difference in proteolytic susceptibility at pH 4.0)
rows.Experimental system: Recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 22-kDa amino-terminal fragments, 0.1 mg/ml, at pH 4.0 in 4.75 M urea; room-temperature limited pepsin digestion at a 2000:1 apoE:pepsin mass ratio; SDS-PAGE and amino-terminal sequencing.

rows.Finding description: Urea denaturation of recombinant human apoE amino-terminal domains at pH 7.4 showed lower unfolding resistance for apoE4 than apoE3, with respective midpoints of 4.3 and 5.2 M urea.
rows.Finding quote: The midpoints of denaturation for the 22-kDa fragments of apoE3 and apoE4 were 5.2 and 4.3 M urea, respectively, consistent with previous results (22) (Fig. 1A).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower urea concentration required for unfolding at pH 7.4)
rows.Experimental system: Bacterially expressed recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 22-kDa amino-terminal fragments; protein incubated overnight at 4 °C across urea concentrations in sodium phosphate buffer, pH 7.4; circular dichroism at 220 nm measured at 25 °C under reducing conditions; no cells, endosomes, or lysosomes.

rows.Finding description: Three-state fitting of acidic-pH denaturation supported stable folding intermediates for both apoE3 and apoE4, without establishing an isoform difference in fit quality.
rows.Finding quote: Therefore, the data were analyzed according to a three-state model (native/intermediate/unfolded) (28), which gave excel- lent fits for the apoE3 and apoE4 isoforms (Fig. 1C) but did not give a better fit for apoE2 than the two-state model.
rows.Finding summary: Both apoE3 and apoE4 acidic-pH unfolding curves were described as excellent fits to the three-state model.
rows.Experimental system: Three-state equilibrium-model analysis of circular-dichroism denaturation data from recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 22-kDa amino-terminal fragments at pH 4.0; same underlying experiment as Fig. 1B.

rows.Finding description: At 0.50 mg/ml, full-length apoE4 had a larger large-species fraction than apoE3, 26% versus 21%, despite identical weight-average sedimentation coefficients of 6.5 S.
rows.Finding quote: Furthermore, at higher protein concentration, large species ( s > 10) were more significantly increased for the apoE4 protein (by 15%), compared to apoE3 protein (6%). These observations support the greater aggregation of apoE4 protein.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (higher fraction of large apoE species at 0.50 mg/ml)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human full-length apoE3 and apoE4 with C-terminal His tags; PBS, pH 7.3; sedimentation velocity at 20°C and 40,000 rpm. Table 2 specifies that its higher-concentration full-length samples were 0.50 mg/ml.
rows.Data location: Fig 4A–B; Table 2, higher-concentration full-length rows and footnote; Table 1

rows.Finding description: Increasing full-length protein concentration from 0.15 to 0.50 mg/ml increased the large-species fraction by 15 percentage points for apoE4 and 6 percentage points for apoE3.
rows.Finding quote: Furthermore, at higher protein concentration, large species ( s > 10) were more significantly increased for the apoE4 protein (by 15%), compared to apoE3 protein (6%).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (greater concentration-dependent increase in large apoE species)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human full-length apoE3 and apoE4; PBS, pH 7.3; 0.15 and 0.50 mg/ml; sedimentation velocity at 20°C and 40,000 rpm.
rows.Data location: Fig 4A–B; Table 2; Results, Size distribution of full-length apoE3 and apoE4 proteins

rows.Finding description: At 1.00 mg/ml, apoE4 72–299 had more large species than apoE3 72–299, 21% versus 12%, and a more heterogeneous distribution; the apoE3 major region contained 77% at 5.9 S.
rows.Finding quote: Similar to the full-length proteins, at higher protein concentrations, apoE4 72-299 had more abundant larger species ( s > 10, 21%), compared with those of apoE3 72-299 (12%). ApoE4 72-299 therefore shows a greater tendency to aggregate.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 72–299 -> apoE4 72–299) -> (higher large-species fraction and greater heterogeneity)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 residues 72–299; 1.00 mg/ml in PBS, pH 7.3; sedimentation velocity at 20°C and 40,000 rpm; continuous c(s) analysis.

rows.Finding description: Increasing concentration from 0.15 to 1.00 mg/ml increased the apoE4 72–299 large-species fraction from 7% to 21%, while the apoE3 fraction changed from 13% to 12%.
rows.Finding quote: The smallest apoE4 72-299 species with s = 4.6 decreased by 4% at the higher protein concentration. At the same time, species s = 6.6 and 9.4 decreased by 24 and 8%, respectively, species s = 7.7 remained at 23%, and those with s > 10 increased by 14%.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 72–299 -> apoE4 72–299) -> (greater concentration-dependent aggregation)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 residues 72–299; 0.15 and 1.00 mg/ml in PBS, pH 7.3; sedimentation velocity at 20°C.

rows.Finding description: At 0.15 mg/ml, apoE4 1–271 contained more large species than apoE3 1–271, 21% versus 13%, with overlapping oligomer distributions spanning approximately 50–400 kDa.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE4 1-271 was made up of more and larger species ( s > 10; 21%), compared to apoE3 1-271 (13%).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 1–271 -> apoE4 1–271) -> (higher fraction of large apoE oligomers)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 residues 1–271; 0.15 mg/ml in PBS, pH 7.3; sedimentation velocity at 20°C; continuous sedimentation and molar-mass distributions.
rows.Data location: Fig 5A–D, dotted curves; Results, Size distribution of C-terminal truncated apoE3 and apoE4 proteins

rows.Finding description: At 1.0 mg/ml, full-length apoE4 had a larger 5.0–15.0 nm particle fraction than apoE3, 46% versus 35%, while both also had a 3.9 nm particle group.
rows.Finding quote: Both apoE3 and E4 proteins showed a distribution with two major particle groups, one with a size of 3.9 nm and another in the range of 5.0–15.0 nm. However, apoE3 had less 5.0–15.0 nm group particles (35%), compared with those of apoE4 (46%).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (higher fraction of larger apoE particles)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human full-length apoE3 and apoE4; 1.0 mg/ml in PBS, pH 7.3; DynaPro-MS/X dynamic light scattering at 20°C, total detection 30–40 minutes per sample.
rows.Data location: Results, Dynamic light scattering of apoE proteins, full-length comparison

rows.Finding description: ApoE4 72–299 showed a 10.0–25.0 nm large-particle group comprising 36% and a 5.1 nm group comprising 62%, whereas apoE3 72–299 had one major 4–10 nm group.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE3 72-299 protein existed as one major particle group in the range of 4–10 nm, whereas apoE4 72-299 showed two major groups with a particle size of 5.1 nm (62%) and another in the range of 10.0–25.0 nm (36%).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 72–299 -> apoE4 72–299) -> (appearance of a larger apoE particle population)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 residues 72–299; 1.0 mg/ml in PBS, pH 7.3; dynamic light scattering at 20°C, 30–40 minutes per sample.
rows.Data location: Results, Dynamic light scattering of apoE proteins, final sentence

rows.Finding description: At 0.15 mg/ml, full-length apoE4 had a smaller large-species fraction than apoE3, 11% versus 15%, although their overall sedimentation distributions were described as very similar.
rows.Finding quote: Size distribution of apoE3 and apoE4 full-length proteins showed very similar patterns ( Fig. 4, A and B ).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (lower fraction of large apoE species at 0.15 mg/ml)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human full-length apoE3 and apoE4, expressed in E. coli BL21(DE3), with C-terminal His tags; lipid-free PBS, pH 7.3; sedimentation velocity at 20°C and 40,000 rpm, continuous c(s) analysis. No cells or endo-lysosomal localization.
rows.Data location: Fig 4A–B; Table 2, full-length proteins at 0.15 mg/ml; Table 1

rows.Finding description: At 0.15 mg/ml, apoE4 72–299 had a smaller large-species fraction than apoE3 72–299, 7% versus 13%, although its overall weight-average sedimentation was higher, 6.4 versus 5.5 S.
rows.Finding quote: After calculating the integration by SEDFIT, both apoE 72-299 proteins showed four species at 0.15 mg/ml protein concentration ( Table 2 ).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 72–299 -> apoE4 72–299) -> (lower large-species fraction but higher overall sedimentation at low concentration)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 residues 72–299, deleting N-terminal helices 1 and 2; 0.15 mg/ml in PBS, pH 7.3; sedimentation velocity at 20°C.

rows.Finding description: At 1.00 mg/ml, the paper reports 10 resolved species for apoE4 72–299 versus five for apoE3 72–299, indicating greater apoE4 distribution complexity.
rows.Finding quote: However, when the protein concentration was increased to 1.00 mg/ml, 10 species were found in apoE4 72-299 protein, compared with five species of apoE3 72-299 ( Fig. 4, E and F ).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 72–299 -> apoE4 72–299) -> (more resolved sedimenting species)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 residues 72–299; 1.00 mg/ml in PBS, pH 7.3; sedimentation velocity at 20°C; distribution regularization confidence 0.68.
rows.Data location: Fig 4E–F; Results, Size distribution of N-terminal truncated apoE3 and apoE4 proteins

rows.Finding description: ApoE4 1–231 had a lower fitted monomer–tetramer dissociation constant than apoE3 1–231, 16 ± 1.3 versus 29 ± 2.8 nM, consistent with stronger tetramerization; isoform-comparison significance was not reported.
rows.Finding quote: The K d of apoE3 1-191 (556 ± 233 nM) was 19 times larger than that of apoE3 1-231 (29 ± 2.8 nM) and 37 times in the case of apoE4 isoforms (592 ± 323 nM of apoE4 1-191 and 16 ± 1.3 nM of apoE4 1-231 ). Both apoE3 1-231 and apoE4 1-231 showed greater tendency toward tetramerization.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 1–231 -> apoE4 1–231) -> (lower modeled tetramer dissociation constant)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 residues 1–231 in PBS, pH 7.3; sedimentation velocity at 20°C fitted with the SEDPHAT monomer–tetramer rapid self-association model.
rows.Data location: Results, Size distribution of C-terminal truncated apoE3 and apoE4 proteins, dissociation-constant paragraph

rows.Finding description: Raising concentration from 0.15 to 1.00 mg/ml reduced the large-species fraction of both 41–299 fragments, from 14% to 10% for apoE4 and from 10% to 9% for apoE3.
rows.Finding quote: However, both apoE 41-299 proteins showed less large species of s > 10 (decreased 1–4%). Neither apoE3 41-299 nor apoE4 41-299 therefore showed a tendency to aggregate.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 41–299 -> apoE4 41–299) -> (no greater concentration-dependent aggregation)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 residues 41–299; 0.15 and 1.00 mg/ml in PBS, pH 7.3; sedimentation velocity at 20°C.
rows.Data location: Fig 4C–D; Table 2; Results, Size distribution of N-terminal truncated apoE3 and apoE4 proteins

rows.Finding description: At 0.15 mg/ml, both apoE3 1–191 and apoE4 1–191 were predominantly monomeric with some tetramer, with no significant isoform difference reported.
rows.Finding quote: Both apoE3 and E4 N-terminal domain (1–191) existed with monomers as the major component together with some tetramer.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 1–191 -> apoE4 1–191) -> (no significant change in monomer/tetramer distribution reported)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 residues 1–191; 0.15 mg/ml in PBS, pH 7.3; sedimentation velocity and c(s)/c(M) analysis at 20°C; estimated species masses approximately 22 and 85 kDa.
rows.Data location: Fig 5A–D, solid curves; Results, Size distribution of C-terminal truncated apoE3 and apoE4 proteins

rows.Finding description: Both apoE3 1–231 and apoE4 1–231 retained monomer and tetramer populations, with no significant isoform difference reported, while adding residues 192–231 increased tetramerization in both.
rows.Finding quote: The two-species distribution was still maintained in the case of the apoE3 1-231 and apoE4 1-231 ( dashed lines in Fig. 5, A and C ), whereas the s values were shifted to 2.4 and 5.5 and the ratio of the two species also changed.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 1–231 -> apoE4 1–231) -> (no significant change in monomer/tetramer distribution reported)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 residues 1–231; 0.15 mg/ml in PBS, pH 7.3; sedimentation velocity and c(s)/c(M) analysis at 20°C; estimated masses approximately 30–35 and 110–140 kDa.
rows.Data location: Fig 5A–D, dashed curves; Results, Size distribution of C-terminal truncated apoE3 and apoE4 proteins

rows.Finding description: The authors report that neither 1–271 fragment showed a significant tendency to aggregate at higher concentration. They give no statistical comparison of the two concentration responses.
rows.Finding quote: However, they did not show a significant tendency to aggregate at higher protein concentration (data not shown).
rows.Finding summary: No significant concentration-dependent aggregation was reported for either 1–271 fragment.
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 residues 1–271; sedimentation-velocity concentration comparison in PBS, pH 7.3, at 20°C; associated experiments used 0.15 and 0.50 mg/ml.
rows.Data location: Results, Size distribution of C-terminal truncated apoE3 and apoE4 proteins, final sentence; data not shown

rows.Finding description: Monomer–tetramer modeling gave similar dissociation constants for apoE3 1–191 and apoE4 1–191, 556 ± 233 and 592 ± 323 nM, with no significant isoform variation reported.
rows.Finding quote: The K d of apoE3 1-191 (556 ± 233 nM) was 19 times larger than that of apoE3 1-231 (29 ± 2.8 nM) and 37 times in the case of apoE4 isoforms (592 ± 323 nM of apoE4 1-191 and 16 ± 1.3 nM of apoE4 1-231 ).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 1–191 -> apoE4 1–191) -> (no significant change in tetramerization affinity reported)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 residues 1–191 in PBS, pH 7.3; sedimentation velocity at 20°C fitted with the SEDPHAT monomer–tetramer rapid self-association model.
rows.Data location: Results, Size distribution of C-terminal truncated apoE3 and apoE4 proteins, dissociation-constant paragraph

rows.Finding description: At 0.15 mg/ml, apoE4 41–299 had a larger broad large-species fraction than apoE3 41–299, 14% versus 10%, while its weight-average sedimentation was lower, 3.7 versus 4.4 S.
rows.Finding quote: After calculating the integration by SEDFIT, five species were identified for both apoE 41-299 proteins ( Table 2 ).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 41–299 -> apoE4 41–299) -> (higher large-species fraction but lower overall sedimentation)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 residues 41–299, deleting N-terminal helix 1; 0.15 mg/ml in PBS, pH 7.3; sedimentation velocity at 20°C and 40,000 rpm.

rows.Finding description: At 1.00 mg/ml, apoE4 41–299 had a large-species fraction of 10% versus 9% for apoE3, and their two major species comprised 72% versus 77%; neither fragment showed a concentration-dependent aggregation tendency.
rows.Finding quote: At an initial protein concentration of 1.00 mg/ml, the major species of apoE3 41-299 with s = 3.7 and 5.0 accounted for 77% of the total amount. In the case of apoE4 41-299 , the major species with s = 3.6 and 5.1 constituted 72% of the total protein amount.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 41–299 -> apoE4 41–299) -> (slightly higher large-species fraction at 1.00 mg/ml)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 residues 41–299; 1.00 mg/ml in PBS, pH 7.3; sedimentation velocity at 20°C and 40,000 rpm.

rows.Finding description: At 0.50 mg/ml, apoE4 72–299 had a higher weight-average sedimentation coefficient than apoE3 72–299, 6.9 versus 5.7 S.
rows.Finding quote: Finally, the s w of the apoE4 72-299 protein had significantly increased (from 6.4 to 7.2) at a higher protein concentration, but apoE3 72-299 did not.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 72–299 -> apoE4 72–299) -> (higher weight-average sedimentation at 0.50 mg/ml)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 residues 72–299; 0.50 mg/ml in PBS, pH 7.3; sedimentation velocity at 20°C.

rows.Finding description: Full-length apoE3 and apoE4 showed no significant difference in weight-average sedimentation: 6.6 versus 6.3 S at 0.15 mg/ml and 6.5 versus 6.5 S at 0.50 mg/ml.
rows.Finding quote: The s w values of apoE and apoE 1-271 proteins were from 6.1 to 6.6 S and did not show any significant difference.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no significant change in full-length apoE weight-average sedimentation)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human full-length apoE3 and apoE4; PBS, pH 7.3; 0.15 and 0.50 mg/ml; sedimentation velocity at 20°C; second-moment integration.
rows.Data location: Table 1, full-length apoE3 and apoE4 rows

rows.Finding description: At 0.15 mg/ml, apoE4 1–231 had a lower weight-average sedimentation coefficient than apoE3 1–231, 3.1 versus 3.8 S.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 1–231 -> apoE4 1–231) -> (lower weight-average sedimentation at 0.15 mg/ml)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 residues 1–231; 0.15 mg/ml in PBS, pH 7.3; sedimentation velocity at 20°C.

rows.Finding description: At 0.50 mg/ml, apoE4 41–299 sedimented more slowly than apoE3 41–299, with weight-average coefficients of 4.3 versus 4.9 S.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE3 41-299 and apoE4 41-299 proteins showed lower s w values (4.4 and 3.7 S) at 0.15 mg/ml and higher s w values (4.8 and 4.3 S) at 0.50 or 1.00 mg/ml, respectively.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 41–299 -> apoE4 41–299) -> (lower weight-average sedimentation at 0.50 mg/ml)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 residues 41–299; 0.50 mg/ml in PBS, pH 7.3; sedimentation velocity at 20°C.

rows.Finding description: At 0.15 mg/ml, apoE4 1–191 had a slightly higher weight-average sedimentation coefficient than apoE3 1–191, 2.7 versus 2.6 S.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 1–191 -> apoE4 1–191) -> (slightly higher weight-average sedimentation at 0.15 mg/ml)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4 residues 1–191; 0.15 mg/ml in PBS, pH 7.3; sedimentation velocity at 20°C.

rows.Finding description: Native PAGE showed greater high-molecular-weight oligomer formation by ApoE4 than ApoE3, with ApoE4 species exceeding 1048 kDa after 24 hours at 37 °C.
rows.Finding quote: Native gel shows the formation of higher oligomeric species for ApoE4 (> 1048 kDa) but not E2 and E3 after incubation at 37°C for 24 h.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (increased high-molecular-weight apoE oligomerization)
rows.Experimental system: Purified full-length recombinant human ApoE from E. coli, incubated in 20 mM phosphate buffer, pH 7.4, at 37 °C for 24 hours; native PAGE, with samples diluted to 3 μM for loading.

rows.Finding description: TEM showed long curved ApoE4 filaments after incubation, whereas ApoE3 formed round species at 24 hours that enlarged and became slightly elongated by three days without mature fibrils.
rows.Finding quote: Small round species were observed at 24 h for ApoE3 that increased in size over time and became slightly elongated after 3-day incubation (Fig. 4c). In contrast, ApoE4 showed fibrillar structures with a curvy appearance at 24 h (Fig. 4c).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (increased formation of mature apoE filaments)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human ApoE in 20 mM phosphate buffer, pH 7.4, incubated at 37 °C for 24 hours or three days; negative-stain TEM using uranyl acetate.

rows.Finding description: TEM showed small round and amorphous species without mature filaments in an equal ApoE3/ApoE4 mixture, whereas ApoE4 alone formed long mature fibrils.
rows.Finding quote: TEM micrographs were produced for the mixed sample and showed the presence of small round and small amorphous species instead of the long mature fibrils observed for ApoE4 alone (Fig. 6b).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE4 alone -> equal apoE3/apoE4 mixture) -> (inhibited mature apoE filament formation)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human ApoE3 and ApoE4, each 12.5 μM, total 25 μM, in phosphate buffer, pH 7.4, incubated 24 hours at 37 °C; negative-stain TEM, compared with ApoE4-alone morphology.
rows.Data location: Fig. 6b (1:1 mixture) and Fig. 4c (ApoE4 alone, 24 h)

rows.Finding description: Baseline native PAGE showed a shared band above 480 kDa but additional ApoE4 multimeric species between 480 and 720 kDa relative to ApoE3.
rows.Finding quote: C. Native PAGE of ApoE isoforms in 20 mM PB showing a common band at >480 kDa, and the presence of higher multimeric species in ApoE4 (between 480 and 720 kDa).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (additional baseline high-molecular-weight apoE multimers)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human ApoE isoforms in 20 mM phosphate buffer; native PAGE; no prolonged incubation specified in this supplementary legend.

rows.Finding description: ThT monitoring over three days showed faster self-assembly-associated fluorescence increases for ApoE4 than ApoE3, although both isoforms eventually showed increases.
rows.Finding quote: Changes in ThT fluorescence varied with each isoform, with a faster increase observed for ApoE4. After 3 days, ApoE3 and ApoE4, but not ApoE2, show changes in ThT fluorescence (top panel).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (faster apoE assembly-associated ThT fluorescence increase)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human ApoE, approximately 25 μM in 20 mM phosphate buffer, pH 7.4, incubated with ThT at 37 °C for three days; fluorescence excitation 440 nm, emission 483 nm, readings every 15 minutes with brief orbital shaking.

rows.Finding description: During the first 24 hours, ApoE4 showed a shorter lag and earlier assembly-associated ThT increase than ApoE3.
rows.Finding quote: The change in fluorescence adjusted to baseline displayed a rapid increase in intensity at 483 nm for ApoE4 (Fig. 4b(i and ii)), and an extended lag phase for ApoE3 before any changes were detected (Fig. 4b(ii).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (shorter lag before apoE assembly-associated ThT fluorescence)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human ApoE, approximately 25 μM in 20 mM phosphate buffer, pH 7.4, with ThT at 37 °C; first 24 hours of the fluorescence time course.

rows.Finding description: Replacing half of a 25 μM ApoE4 sample with ApoE3 reduced the assembly-associated ThT increase relative to ApoE4 alone, producing kinetics distinct from ApoE3 alone.
rows.Finding quote: Figure 6a shows that ApoE3 reduced the rate of assembly of ApoE4, measured by ThT fluorescence; the ThT kinetics of the mixed sample did not resemble that of E3 alone either.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE4 alone -> equal apoE3/apoE4 mixture) -> (reduced apoE assembly-associated ThT kinetics)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human ApoE in 20 mM phosphate buffer, pH 7.4, incubated at 37 °C for 24 hours; ApoE3 alone or ApoE4 alone at 25 μM versus 12.5 μM of each isoform; ThT fluorescence.

rows.Finding description: Before-versus-after ThT scans were reported to show a significant three-day fluorescence change only for ApoE4, rather than ApoE3, indicating greater ApoE4 self-assembly.
rows.Finding quote: Comparison between ThT fluorescence scans taken before and after a 3-day incubation period shows significant differences in signal only for ApoE4, indicative of self-assembly.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (greater incubation-associated ThT signal change)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human ApoE isoforms incubated with ThT for three days at 37 °C in 20 mM phosphate buffer, pH 7.4; fluorescence scans before and after incubation.

rows.Finding description: After dialysis into phosphate buffer, ApoE3 and ApoE4 showed no significant difference reported in baseline sedimentation or oligomer distributions.
rows.Finding quote: AUC revealed no differences in sedimentation velocity between the three isoforms in either buffer (Fig. S3, Fig. 1c and d, Table 2a), and the major species was characterized with a molecular mass of 130 kDa (Table 2a).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in baseline oligomerization after phosphate-buffer dialysis)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human ApoE, 8 μM, dialyzed into 20 mM phosphate buffer, pH 7.4; analytical ultracentrifugation at 20 °C and 40,000 rpm.

rows.Finding description: Sedimentation profiles in phosphate buffer showed no significant difference reported between ApoE3 and ApoE4 in baseline oligomerization.
rows.Finding quote: AUC revealed no differences in sedimentation velocity between the three isoforms in either buffer (Fig. S3, Fig. 1c and d, Table 2a), and the major species was characterized with a molecular mass of 130 kDa (Table 2a).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in baseline oligomerization in phosphate buffer)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human ApoE, 8 μM in 20 mM phosphate buffer, pH 7.4; analytical ultracentrifugation at 20 °C, 40,000 rpm; Lamm-equation fitting and residual analysis.

rows.Finding description: SEC-MALS showed no significant difference reported in baseline oligomerization between recombinant ApoE3 and ApoE4, with peak molecular masses of 139 and 151 kDa, respectively, interpreted as tetramers.
rows.Finding quote: All ApoE isoforms have identical elution volumes, and a MW of 145, 139 and 151 kDa is calculated at elution peak for ApoE2, ApoE3 and ApoE4, respectively.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in baseline tetrameric oligomerization)
rows.Experimental system: Purified full-length recombinant human ApoE from E. coli; SEC-MALS at room temperature using 5 mg/mL protein in 20 mM HEPES, 300 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP, pH 8.0.

rows.Finding description: SEC of purified recombinant human ApoE isoforms showed no significant difference reported between ApoE3 and ApoE4 in their baseline elution pattern, consistent with similar oligomerization.
rows.Finding quote: Gel filtration and size exclusion chromatography (SEC) coupled with multi-angle light scattering (SEC-MALS) showed multimerization of all three proteins consistent with a tetramer in solution with a molecular weight (MW) of 139–151 kDa (Fig. 1a and b, Table 1).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in baseline oligomerization detected by SEC)
rows.Experimental system: Full-length recombinant human ApoE expressed in E. coli Rosetta2(DE3), purified by affinity chromatography and SEC; Superdex 200 chromatography in 20 mM HEPES, 300 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, pH 8.0; no cells or endo-lysosomal compartment.

rows.Finding description: SAXS analysis supported no significant difference reported in baseline oligomerization or dimensions between ApoE3 and ApoE4, despite molecular-mass estimates of 160 ± 5 and 169 ± 4 kDa.
rows.Finding quote: Together AUC, SEC-MALS and SAXS show that the three ApoE isoforms are similar in size, shape and multimerization, and all form tetrameric species in solution.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in interpreted SAXS-derived baseline oligomerization)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human ApoE analyzed by SEC-SAXS at 20 °C in HEPES/NaCl buffer, pH 8.0; ATSAS and ScÅtter analysis, including volume-of-correlation mass estimates.

rows.Finding description: Gel-filtration estimates were shared across ApoE3 and ApoE4 with no significant difference reported, including an apparent mass of 333 kDa and Stokes radius of 5.8 nm.
rows.Finding quote: A hydrodynamic radius of 5.8–6.5 nm was calculated for each isoform, and a frictional ratio f/f0 above 1.7 suggests elongated shape for the homotetramers (Table 1).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in reported gel-filtration oligomer properties)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human ApoE isoforms analyzed on calibrated Superdex 200 in HEPES/NaCl/glycerol SEC buffer, pH 8.0; apparent mass and hydrodynamic properties inferred from elution.

rows.Finding description: The Discussion reports ApoE4 fibrils dissociating to monomers on SDS-PAGE and no significant difference reported in native-gel mobility between ApoE4 species and ApoE3, despite the earlier high-molecular-weight native-PAGE result.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE4 fibrils run as a monomer by SDS page (data not shown) and the ApoE4 species run on a native gel at similar mobility to ApoE3 and ApoE2.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in native-gel mobility reported in Discussion)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human ApoE; SDS-PAGE of ApoE4 fibrils and native electrophoresis comparing ApoE species; precise sample timing and handling are unspecified for this Discussion statement.
rows.Data location: Discussion sentence: ApoE4 fibrils run as a monomer by SDS page (data not shown) and the ApoE4 species run on a native gel at similar mobility to ApoE3 and ApoE2.

rows.Finding description: Comparison of ApoE4 SAXS data with ApoE3 showed no significant difference reported in baseline scattering profiles or overall tetramer architecture.
rows.Finding quote: All three proteins exhibited identical scattering profiles indicating that they are very similar in shape (Fig. 2a–c).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in baseline oligomer architecture detected by SAXS)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human ApoE; inline SEC-SAXS at 20 °C, loaded at 10 mg/mL, in 20 mM HEPES and 300 mM NaCl, pH 8.0; Fig 2C compared with Fig 2B.

rows.Finding description: SAXS pair-distance distributions showed no significant difference reported between ApoE3 and ApoE4 in their extended baseline oligomer shape.
rows.Finding quote: This elongated shape is reproduced in the pair distance distribution function and fits to a maximal dimension of approximately 19.5 nm (195 Å) (Fig. 2d).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in baseline oligomer dimensions)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human ApoE analyzed by inline SEC-SAXS at 20 °C in 20 mM HEPES and 300 mM NaCl, pH 8.0; pair-distance distribution analysis.

rows.Finding description: APOE4–mCh showed significantly greater colocalization with LAMP1-marked lysosomes than APOE3–mCh in human HEK293 cells, using three wells per isoform.
rows.Finding quote: Imaris analysis revealed that APOE4–mCh cells had significantly higher colocalization between APOE and lysosomes, and significantly greater average surface area of individual lysosomal and APOE puncta (Fig. 3A) than did APOE3–mCh cells, suggesting greater trafficking to lysosomes.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (greater APOE–lysosome colocalization)
rows.Experimental system: Human HEK293 cells, ATCC CRL-1573; stable APOE3–mCherry versus APOE4–mCherry expression; transient CellLight LAMP1–GFP lysosomal labeling; live confocal microscopy and Imaris colocalization analysis; three images per well.

rows.Finding description: Dual-tagged APOE4 produced a significantly lower green-to-red fluorescence ratio than APOE3 in human HEK293 cells, indicating greater acidic lysosomal localization using three wells per isoform.
rows.Finding quote: APOE4–mCh–SepH cells had a significantly lower ratio of green to red fluorescence compared with APOE3–mCh–SepH cells, indicating a greater degree of lysosomal localization of the protein (Fig. 3B).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower green-to-red reporter ratio, indicating greater lysosomal APOE localization)
rows.Experimental system: Human HEK293 cells, ATCC CRL-1573; stable expression of APOE3–mCherry–SepHluorin versus APOE4–mCherry–SepHluorin; live confocal imaging and Imaris fluorescence-area analysis; three images per well. Acid-sensitive SepHluorin is quenched in acidic compartments.

rows.Finding description: After uptake into rat ST14A cells, APOE4 showed significantly greater colocalization with late than early endosomes whereas APOE3 did not, using three wells per genotype without a reported direct between-isoform significance test.
rows.Finding quote: APOE4 colocalized with late endosomes significantly more than with early endosomes, whereas APOE3 did not.
rows.Finding summary: (extracellular APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (late-over-early endosomal localization preference observed for APOE4)
rows.Experimental system: Immortalized rat neuron-like ST14A cells; 24 h exposure to conditioned medium containing human APOE3–mCherry or APOE4–mCherry; fixed-cell staining for mCherry and early-endosomal EEA1 or late-endosomal Rab7; confocal imaging and Imaris colocalization analysis.

rows.Finding description: During bafilomycin treatment, APOE4–mCh fluorescence increased more strongly over time than APOE3–mCh fluorescence in human HEK293 cells, with four wells per treatment.
rows.Finding quote: There was a significant difference between slopes of APOE3–mCh and APOE4–mCh fluorescence treated with Baf over time when analyzed by linear regression, suggesting that APOE4–mCh fluorescence is more strongly affected by Baf and is turned over more rapidly by the lysosome.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (greater fluorescence accumulation during lysosomal inhibition)
rows.Experimental system: Human HEK293 cells, ATCC CRL-1573; stable clonal APOE3–mCherry versus APOE4–mCherry expression; bafilomycin A1 treatment, 50 nM; live-cell fluorescence time course and linear-regression comparison of slopes. The figure legend specifies a 4 h treatment.

rows.Finding description: Rat neuron-like ST14A cells accumulated more intracellular red fluorescence from APOE4–mCh than APOE3–mCh conditioned medium during the uptake time course, using three wells per medium genotype.
rows.Finding quote: Internalization levels were isoform-dependent, with the highest fluorescence observed in both cell types treated with APOE4–mCh, and the lowest in APOE2–mCh-treated cells (Fig. 7A,B).
rows.Finding summary: (extracellular APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher intracellular APOE-associated fluorescence during uptake)
rows.Experimental system: Immortalized rat neuronally derived ST14A cells, supplied by Elena Cattaneo's laboratory; no endogenous APOE detected by western blot; human HEK293T conditioned medium containing APOE3–mCherry or APOE4–mCherry, mixed 1:1 with fresh medium; IncuCyte fluorescence normalized to phase area over time. Endpoint duration is not stated in the supplied Fig 7B text.

rows.Finding description: In human HEK293 cells, APOE4–mCh had significantly higher whole-cell protein abundance than APOE3–mCh, measured using four wells per genotype.
rows.Finding quote: APOE4–mCh cells have significantly higher APOE levels by western blot (Fig. 1A) and fluorescence (Fig. 2) than APOE3–mCh, in spite of similar APOE RNA levels (Fig. S1Ai).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher intracellular APOE protein abundance)
rows.Experimental system: Human embryonic kidney HEK293 cells, ATCC CRL-1573; one selected stable clonal line per APOE–mCherry construct; baseline whole-cell western blotting. These are not brain cells; no aging or AD model was specified.

rows.Finding description: Bafilomycin significantly increased APOE4–mCh protein abundance in human HEK293 cells, testing lysosomal degradation within a fixed APOE4 background using three wells per treatment.
rows.Finding quote: Baf treatment significantly increased the abundance of APOE3–mCh and APOE4–mCh (Fig. 1B), and red fluorescence of APOE3–mCh and APOE4–mCh cells (Fig. 2).
rows.Finding summary: (lysosomal inhibition in APOE4 cells) -> (higher intracellular APOE4 protein abundance)
rows.Experimental system: Human HEK293 cells, ATCC CRL-1573, stably expressing APOE4–mCherry; bafilomycin A1, 50 nM for 4 h, versus untreated cells; whole-cell western blotting.

rows.Finding description: APOE4–mCh-expressing human HEK293 cells had significantly higher baseline red fluorescence than APOE3–mCh cells, with four wells per treatment.
rows.Finding quote: APOE4–mCh cells have significantly higher APOE levels by western blot (Fig. 1A) and fluorescence (Fig. 2) than APOE3–mCh, in spite of similar APOE RNA levels (Fig. S1Ai).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher intracellular APOE-associated fluorescence)
rows.Experimental system: Human HEK293 cells, ATCC CRL-1573; stable clonal APOE3–mCherry versus APOE4–mCherry expression; live-cell fluorescence imaging. Fluorescence measures intracellular abundance, not an aggregate-specific signal.

rows.Finding description: Bafilomycin significantly increased intracellular APOE4–mCh red fluorescence in human HEK293 cells, testing lysosomal degradation within a fixed APOE4 background using four wells per treatment.
rows.Finding quote: Baf treatment significantly increased the abundance of APOE3–mCh and APOE4–mCh (Fig. 1B), and red fluorescence of APOE3–mCh and APOE4–mCh cells (Fig. 2).
rows.Finding summary: (lysosomal inhibition in APOE4 cells) -> (higher intracellular APOE4-associated fluorescence)
rows.Experimental system: Human HEK293 cells, ATCC CRL-1573, stably expressing APOE4–mCherry; bafilomycin A1, 50 nM, versus untreated cells; live-cell fluorescence imaging. The figure legend specifies a 4 h treatment.

rows.Finding description: Rapamycin significantly increased APOE4–mCh protein abundance in human HEK293 cells, testing autophagy modulation within a fixed APOE4 background using three wells per treatment.
rows.Finding quote: Whereas Rap treatment significantly increased the LC3II/LC3I ratio (Fig. 1B), suggesting that LC3-dependent autophagy was effectively stimulated, Rap did not significantly reduce APOE levels. Instead, the abundance of APOE4–mCh significantly increased (Fig. 1B).
rows.Finding summary: (rapamycin treatment in APOE4 cells) -> (higher intracellular APOE4 protein abundance)
rows.Experimental system: Human HEK293 cells, ATCC CRL-1573, stably expressing APOE4–mCherry; rapamycin, 10 nM for 4 h, versus untreated cells; whole-cell western blotting.

rows.Finding description: After uptake into rat ST14A cells, 22% of LC3A/B spots colocalized with APOE4 versus 17% with APOE3, using four wells per genotype; between-isoform significance was not reported.
rows.Finding quote: Colocalization of APOE with LC3A and/or LC3B was observed, with 17% of LC3A and LC3B spots colocalizing with APOE3–mCh and 22% colocalizing with APOE4–mCH spots (Fig. S8C).
rows.Finding summary: (extracellular APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher reported fraction of LC3A/B spots colocalizing with APOE)
rows.Experimental system: Immortalized rat neuron-like ST14A cells; 24 h exposure to conditioned medium containing human APOE3–mCherry or APOE4–mCherry; endogenous LC3A/B and mCherry immunostaining; confocal microscopy and Imaris spot analysis, defining colocalization by centers within 1 μm; four images per well. LC3 association does not establish lysosomal localization or APOE aggregation.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Fig S8C; Supplementary Table S5

rows.Finding description: Whole-cell fractionation immunoblots showed greater relative amounts of aggregated apoE in ApoE4 than ApoE3 primary mouse astrocytes, with three independent experiments reported for the associated quantification.
rows.Finding quote: The relative amount of aggregated ABCA1 and ApoE were significantly increased in ApoE4 primary astrocytes compared with ApoE3 primary astrocytes ( Fig. 4 D , E ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (increased aggregated apoE in primary mouse astrocytes)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical astrocytes from 1–3-day-old mice homozygous for human APOE3 or APOE4 targeted replacement, backcrossed onto C57BL/6J for 10 generations; cultures approximately 95% astrocytes. Whole-cell lysates were separated into RIPA-soluble and RIPA-insoluble, guanidine-HCl-soluble fractions and immunoblotted for apoE. No endosomal or lysosomal localization of apoE aggregates was measured.

rows.Finding description: Hippocampal fractionation immunoblots showed greater relative amounts of aggregated apoE in male ApoE4-TR mice (n=8) than ApoE3-TR mice (n=6).
rows.Finding quote: In agreement, the relative amounts of aggregated ABCA1 and ApoE were greater in hippocampal homogenates of male ApoE4-TR mice ( n = 8) compared with ApoE3-TR mice ( n = 6) ( Fig. 4 F , G ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (increased aggregated apoE in mouse hippocampus)
rows.Experimental system: Age-matched, 4-month-old male mice homozygous for human APOE3 or APOE4 targeted replacement on a C57BL/6J background. Hippocampal homogenates were separated into RIPA-soluble and guanidine-HCl-soluble fractions and immunoblotted for apoE; cell type and subcellular location of aggregates were not resolved.

rows.Finding description: Recombinant apoE4 formed numerically more aggregates than apoE3 after four hours at 37°C, but there was no significant difference (p=0.2); three independent experiments were reported for the associated quantification.
rows.Finding quote: rApoE4 protein formed more aggregates than rApoE3 protein when incubated ex vivo for 4 h at 37°C, although the observed increase in ApoE4 aggregation were not statistically significant ( p = 0.2; Fig. 4 H , I ).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in recombinant apoE aggregation reaching statistical significance)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4, 10 μg each, incubated in RIPA buffer at 37°C for four hours; RIPA-soluble and guanidine-HCl-soluble fractions assessed by anti-apoE Western blot. This was neither an acidic-pH nor an endo-lysosomal experiment.

rows.Finding description: Quantification of three independent recombinant-protein experiments found no significant difference in aggregation between apoE4 and apoE3 after four hours at 37°C (p=0.2), despite a numerical increase for apoE4.
rows.Finding quote: rApoE4 protein formed more aggregates than rApoE3 protein when incubated ex vivo for 4 h at 37°C, although the observed increase in ApoE4 aggregation were not statistically significant ( p = 0.2; Fig. 4 H , I ).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in recombinant apoE aggregation reaching statistical significance)
rows.Experimental system: Recombinant human apoE3 versus apoE4, 10 μg per preparation, incubated in RIPA buffer for four hours at 37°C; densitometric quantification of Western blots of RIPA-soluble and guanidine-HCl-soluble fractions. No cells, acidic-pH manipulation, or organelle localization.

rows.Finding description: CSF fractionation immunoblots from age- and sex-matched APOE ε4/ε4 carriers (n=5) and ε3/ε3 carriers (n=6) showed a 2.5-fold greater percentage of aggregated apoE in ε4/ε4 CSF.
rows.Finding quote: We then examined ApoE protein aggregation in human CSF from age and sex matched APOE ε3/ε3 ( n = 6) and ε4/ε4 ( n = 5) carriers. The results revealed greater percentage of aggregated ApoE protein in CSF of ε4/ε4 carriers (2.5-fold increased) compared with ε3/ε3 carriers ( Fig. 4 J , K ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE ε3/ε3 -> APOE ε4/ε4) -> (increased aggregated apoE percentage in human CSF)
rows.Experimental system: Human CSF from six APOE ε3/ε3 and five APOE ε4/ε4 age- and sex-matched carriers; RIPA-soluble and guanidine-HCl-soluble apoE detected by Western blot, with Ponceau staining as loading control. This measures extracellular CSF apoE, without identifying its source cell or endo-lysosomal localization; ages are not supplied for this aggregation cohort.

rows.Finding description: Western blotting of anterior cingulate cortex detergent-solubilized pellets from two human siblings, one APOE4 homozygote and one APOE3 homozygote, showed more high-molecular-weight apoE-containing complexes and apoE fragments in the APOE4 sibling.
rows.Finding quote: However, apoE fragments and larger complexes in ACC were more abundant in Patient 1 (Figure 2F).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3/3 -> APOE4/4) -> (more high-molecular-weight apoE-containing complexes in anterior cingulate cortex)
rows.Experimental system: Postmortem human anterior cingulate cortex from two siblings with C9ORF72 repeat expansions and familial FTLD-MND, one APOE ε4/ε4 and one APOE ε3/ε3. Reported ages at death were 61 and 60 years, respectively; demographic information was modified for privacy. Postmortem collection intervals were 12.8 and 6.5 hours, respectively. Detergent-solubilized pellet fractions were analyzed by SDS–PAGE and anti-human apoE western blotting, with 10 μg protein per lane. No cell-type or endosomal/lysosomal localization was measured.

rows.Finding description: During recombinant-protein incubation, apoE3 disaggregated into monomers whereas apoE4 aggregates remained stable for up to four hours and subsequently precipitated, with 30% of apoE4 disappearing from solution by 48 hours; three to four experiments were reported per isoform.
rows.Finding quote: Under these conditions, apoE3 consistently disaggregated into monomers, whereas apoE2 and apoE4 aggregates were stable for up to 4 hours, thereafter gradually precipitating onto the walls of the sample vial. By 48 hours, 70% of the apoE2 and 30% of the apoE4 disappeared from solution (Fig. 3).
rows.Finding summary: (recombinant apoE3 -> recombinant apoE4) -> (greater aggregate persistence and less dissociation into monomers)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free recombinant human apoE3 versus apoE4 at 1.0 μg/mL (29 nM), incubated at 35°C with 1 μg/mL micellar cholesterol and protease inhibitors; time-course size-exclusion HPLC A280 profiles. Chromatography used pH 6.65 eluent; no endosomal or lysosomal cellular compartment was studied.
rows.Data location: Fig. 3B; Fig. 3C; Results subsection 'ApoE3 more readily dissociates from aggregates'

rows.Finding description: Following neprilysin inhibition, APOE4 mice showed greater apoE co-localization with large CA1 neuronal lysosomes than the other groups, with about 6% of accumulated intracellular apoE4 localized there and no corresponding localization to small lysosomes.
rows.Finding quote: As shown in Figure 4C, apoE accumulated specifically in the CA1 neurons of the thiorphan-treated apoE4 mice (P < 0.03 for treated apoE4 compared to other mouse groups), and the accumulated apoE4 co-localized preferentially with the large lysosomes (P < 0.03 for treated apoE4 compared to the other mouse groups) but not with the small ones. About 6% of the accumulated intracellular apoE4 co-localized with the large lysosomes.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (increased apoE accumulation in large neuronal lysosomes following neprilysin inhibition)
rows.Experimental system: Three- to four-month-old male human APOE3- or APOE4-homozygous targeted-replacement mice, backcrossed eight generations to C57BL/6J; hippocampal CA1 neurons following intracerebroventricular thiorphan or sham treatment; confocal apoE/Cathepsin D co-localization, separating small lysosomes of 0.2–0.5 μm2 from large lysosomes of 0.5–2 μm2.
rows.Data location: Fig 4C, small- and large-lysosomal apoE measurements

rows.Finding description: After neprilysin inhibition, APOE4 mice had greater large-lysosomal co-localization of apoE with Aβ42 than APOE3 mice, measuring apoE-containing co-localized material without establishing apoE self-aggregation.
rows.Finding quote: As shown in Figure 4D, quadruple labeling (Aβ42, I-11, CatD, and apoE4) revealed co-localization of lysosomal apoE with Aβ42 (yellow arrowheads) and with oligo-Aβ42 (yellow arrows). Furthermore, co-localization of these aggregates with large lysosomes was specifically elevated in the thiorphan-treated apoE4 mice (P < 0.02 for the treated apoE4 compared to other mouse groups) (Fig. 4D).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (increased lysosomal apoE/Aβ42 co-localization following neprilysin inhibition)
rows.Experimental system: Three- to four-month-old male human APOE3- or APOE4-homozygous targeted-replacement mice on an eight-generation C57BL/6J backcross background; hippocampal CA1 neurons after intracerebroventricular thiorphan; quadruple confocal labeling for apoE, Aβ42, I-11, and Cathepsin D; treatment duration not separately stated for panel D.

rows.Finding description: In the genotype-subtracted analysis, apoE4-specific apoE occupancy was undetectable in large lysosomes and mitochondria at day 4 but greater in large lysosomes than mitochondria at day 7, providing a compartment comparison of apoE accumulation.
rows.Finding quote: This comparison revealed that by day 4 about 4% of the mitochondria and no lysosomes were occupied by Aβ, and that at this time point these organelles did not contain either oligo-Aβ42 or apoE4. In contrast, at later time points (e.g. at day 7), occupancy of the large lysosomes by Aβ and apoE was greater than that of the mitochondria (P < 0.005 and P < 0.01, respectively), and both organelles contained similar amounts of oligo-Aβ42 (Fig. 6).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (preferential large-lysosomal apoE occupancy by day 7 following neprilysin inhibition)
rows.Experimental system: Three- to four-month-old male human APOE3- and APOE4-homozygous targeted-replacement mice, backcrossed eight generations to C57BL/6J; hippocampal CA1 neurons after intracerebroventricular thiorphan; confocal co-localization results from Figures 4–5, subtracting mean APOE3 co-localized area from APOE4 values and normalizing to organelle area.
rows.Data location: Fig 6, apoE-containing organelle occupancy at days 4 and 7

rows.Finding description: A2E plus complement exposure increased the fraction of large apoE3 condensates but produced no stress-induced increase in apoE4 condensates in primary porcine RPE, opposing greater stress-induced condensation of apoE4; 15–29 cells were analyzed per condition.
rows.Finding quote: We also observed a small but significant increase in large condensates in ApoE3-RPE exposed to A2E and NHS, whereas ApoE4-RPE were completely resistant to this stress-induced phase separation (Figure 5A).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (resistance to stress-induced enlargement of intracellular apoE condensates)
rows.Experimental system: Primary adult porcine RPE monolayers expressing human mCherry-tagged apoE3 or apoE4; A2E treatment at 10 μM for 6 hours followed by a 48-hour chase, with normal human serum as a complement source. Live confocal imaging and 3D reconstruction measured the percentage of apoE condensates exceeding 0.6 μm3. Endo-lysosomal localization was not established.

rows.Finding description: Baseline apoE4 condensates had a higher printed mean volume than apoE3 condensates in primary porcine RPE, 0.3233 versus 0.2596 μm3, respectively; the printed medians were also higher, 0.15 versus 0.12 μm3, but comparative significance was not reported.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE4 M ean = 0 .3 2 3 3 µm3 M edian = 0 .1 5 µm3
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher baseline mean intracellular apoE condensate volume)
rows.Experimental system: Primary adult porcine RPE monolayers transiently expressing human mCherry-tagged apoE3 or apoE4; baseline live confocal imaging and 3D surface reconstruction, with condensate-volume histograms generated in Matlab. These are intracellular condensates without demonstrated endo-lysosomal localization, not human brain-cell aggregates.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Fig S4E, ApoE3 histogram; Supplementary Fig S4F, ApoE4 histogram

rows.Finding description: The reported significant large-condensate comparisons were ApoE2 versus ApoE3 or ApoE4. For ApoE4 versus ApoE3, the companion histograms show descriptively higher mean and median baseline volumes, with no reported pairwise significance.
rows.Finding quote: Although the 3 isoforms had similar disorder tendencies when analyzed by meta-predictors such as DisMeta (49) and other commonly used disorder predictors (Supplemental Figure 4, A–C), there were significantly more ApoE2 condensates with larger volumes (>0.6 μm3), compared with either ApoE3 or ApoE4 condensates (Figure 4D and Supplemental Figure 4, D–F).
rows.Finding summary: ApoE4 had higher descriptive mean and median baseline condensate volumes than ApoE3. The fraction above 0.6 μm³ has no stated ApoE4-versus-ApoE3 result.
rows.Experimental system: Primary adult porcine RPE monolayers transiently expressing human mCherry-tagged apoE3 or apoE4; baseline live confocal imaging, Imaris 3D surface reconstruction and condensate-volume frequency distributions. No endosomal or lysosomal markers were used for this readout.
rows.Data location: Fig 4D for volume-frequency distributions and sample-size range; Supplementary Fig S4E–F for ApoE3 and ApoE4 means and medians

rows.Finding description: Live imaging showed that both human apoE3 and apoE4 formed spherical intracellular condensate-like structures in primary porcine RPE, without establishing an apoE4-versus-apoE3 difference in aggregation in this panel.
rows.Finding quote: Live-cell imaging showed that ApoE forms spherical structures with average sphericity approximately 0.9 (Figure 4, A and B) that readily fuse and relax (Figure 4C), suggesting that ApoE2, ApoE3, and ApoE4 all segregate into liquid-like assemblies within the RPE.
rows.Finding summary: Intracellular condensates were visible with both ApoE3 and ApoE4. This shared presence gives no direction for a difference in aggregation burden.
rows.Experimental system: Primary adult porcine retinal pigment epithelial cells isolated from freshly harvested eyes, plated as confluent monolayers and transiently expressing human mCherry-tagged apoE3 or apoE4; imaged 48–72 hours after transfection by live spinning-disc confocal microscopy with 3D surface reconstruction. No endosomal or lysosomal localization was established, and these were not human brain cells.

rows.Finding description: Negative-stain electron microscopy showed larger LPS-induced APOE4 aggregates than APOE3 aggregates at a reported 1:1 molar ratio.
rows.Finding quote: The findings from the shift assay were further corroborated through transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with negative staining, which demonstrated the formation of aggregates when rAPOE isoforms were exposed to LPS. Notably, rAPOE4 complexes were larger than those formed with APOE3 when mixed with LPS at a 1:1 M ratio (Fig. 6A).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (larger LPS-induced APOE aggregates)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human APOE3 and APOE4 with E. coli LPS; cell-free negative-stain TEM after 30 minutes at 37 °C; methods specify 5 μM protein and 5 μM endotoxin, while Fig 6A legend specifies 10 μM LPS; three independent preparations.

rows.Finding description: Image analysis of electron micrographs found a larger mean-complex-area distribution for LPS-treated APOE4 than APOE3.
rows.Finding quote: This difference in aggregate size was confirmed by image analysis, revealing a larger distribution of the mean complex area in samples containing rAPOE4 compared with rAPOE3 (Fig. 6B).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (larger LPS-induced APOE aggregate area)
rows.Experimental system: ImageJ analysis of negative-stain TEM images of purified recombinant human APOE3 and APOE4 with E. coli LPS; three independently prepared samples, ten fields examined per preparation; 30-minute incubation at 37 °C; reported size metric differs between Results and methods.

rows.Finding description: After LPS exposure, APOE4 showed higher ThT-inferred β-sheet content than APOE3, with the legend specifically describing an APOE4 response at 5 μM LPS absent for APOE3.
rows.Finding quote: Notably, rAPOE4 exhibited a higher β-sheet content, both in isolation and when exposed to LPS, compared with the rAPOE3 isoform (Fig. 6C).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher LPS-associated ThT-inferred amyloid-like APOE aggregation)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human APOE3 and APOE4, 5 μM, with E. coli LPS at 5, 10, or 20 μM in 10 mM Tris, pH 7.4; 30 minutes at 37 °C, then 100 μM ThT for 15 minutes; fluorescence readout; four independent experiments.

rows.Finding description: Fluorescence microscopy found a higher Amytracker aggregate signal for LPS-treated APOE4 than APOE3 and showed LPS within the stained aggregates.
rows.Finding quote: With this fluorescent probe, an increase in fluorescence signal was detected in rAPOE4 compared with rAPOE3 (5 μM) exposed to 5 μM of E. coli LPS (Fig. 7).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher LPS-associated Amytracker-positive APOE aggregate signal)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human APOE3 and APOE4, 5 μM, exposed to E. coli LPS-FITC and stained with Amytracker 680; fluorescence microscopy; methods specify 5 μM LPS-FITC for 30 minutes at 37 °C followed by staining for 30 minutes at room temperature, whereas legend specifies 10 μM LPS-FITC; three independent experiments.

rows.Finding description: Blue-native electrophoresis showed an APOE4 shift toward larger complexes at a 1:1 protein:LPS ratio, whereas APOE3 signal loss at 1:2 was attributed to complexes too large to enter the gel.
rows.Finding quote: We noted a significant shift toward higher molecular complexes when rAPOE4 was combined with LPS at a molecular ratio of 1:1. Furthermore, we observed a substantial reduction in the signal for rAPOE3 following LPS exposure at a molecular ratio of 1:2. This decrease in signal may be attributed to the formation of very high molecular weight complexes involving APOE, which are unable to enter the BN gel.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (greater apparent complex formation at lower LPS exposure)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human APOE3 and APOE4, 5 μM, with E. coli LPS at protein:LPS ratios 1:1, 1:2, and 1:4 in 10 mM Tris, pH 7.4; blue-native PAGE followed by anti-APOE Western blotting; four independent experiments; legend specifies 30 minutes at room temperature, methods 30 minutes at 37 °C.

rows.Finding description: Mouse macrophages took up significantly more Amytracker-stained LPS-treated APOE4 aggregates than APOE3 aggregates in four independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: Furthermore, the data indicate that uptake by the cells was significantly more pronounced for the LPS-treated E4 isoform when compared with the LPS-treated E3 isoform (Fig. 8A).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (greater macrophage-associated uptake of APOE aggregates)
rows.Experimental system: Murine RAW 264.7 macrophage cell line, passages 4–7; recombinant human APOE3 or APOE4, 100 nM, with E. coli LPS, 100 nM, and Amytracker 680; mixtures incubated 30 minutes at room temperature before 1-hour cell exposure at 37 °C; fluorescence after washing; no endosomal or lysosomal marker.

rows.Finding description: Electron microscopy showed increased aggregates after lipid-A exposure for APOE3, whereas APOE4 did not show the corresponding effect observed with Pseudomonas LPS.
rows.Finding quote: We observed an increase in protein aggregates when rAPOE3 was exposed to both LPS from P. aeruginosa and lipid A from E. coli. However, we did not observe the same effect in the protein aggregates of rAPOE4 when challenged by lipid A from E. coli compared with LPS from P. aeruginosa (Fig. S4).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (reduced apparent aggregation response to isolated lipid A)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human APOE3 and APOE4, 5 μM, exposed to P. aeruginosa LPS, E. coli lipid A, or Tris buffer; negative-stain TEM; methods describe 5 μM endotoxin, 30 minutes at 37 °C, ten fields per grid across three independent preparations; no cells or endo-lysosomal localization.

rows.Finding description: Amytracker microscopy detected no aggregate formation by either APOE3 or APOE4 alone, providing a qualitative baseline null without a reported statistical isoform comparison.
rows.Finding quote: It is important to note that rAPOE isoforms alone did not exhibit the formation of aggregates (Fig. S5).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (no change in detectable baseline aggregates by Amytracker microscopy)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human APOE3 and APOE4, 5 μM, without LPS; Amytracker 680 fluorescence microscopy; three independent experiments; cell-free assay, no acidic or endo-lysosomal compartment.

rows.Finding description: At 0.5 mg/ml, recombinant human apoE4 predominantly formed high-molecular-mass aggregates within 4 hours at 37 °C, whereas most apoE3 remained tetrameric even after 24 hours.
rows.Finding quote: By 4 h of incubation at 37 oC, apoE4 mostly eluted in the void volume of the column, indicating pronounced self-association into higher molecular mass oligomers (Figure 1c). These aggregates were soluble with no obvious turbidity and did not pellet in a microcentrifuge (13,000 g; 30 min). ApoE3 and apoE2 aggregated far more slowly. Even after 24 h at 37 oC, most of the apoE2 or apoE3 remained tetrameric (Figure 1c
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (faster formation of high-molecular-mass apoE aggregates)
rows.Experimental system: Purified, lipid-free recombinant human apoE expressed in E. coli; gel-filtration-isolated low-mass material termed tetramer by the authors; 0.5 mg/ml in 100 mM NH4HCO3, pH 7.8, incubated at 37 °C and assessed by analytical gel filtration. Comparable behavior was reported in PBS and TBS at pH 7.4. This was an acellular experiment without endosomal or lysosomal localization.

rows.Finding description: At 0.2 mg/ml, recombinant human apoE4 aggregated faster than apoE3 and mostly formed high-molecular-mass aggregates within 4 hours at 37 °C.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE3 and apoE2 aggregated far more slowly. Even after 24 h at 37 oC, most of the apoE2 or apoE3 remained tetrameric (Figure 1c). The rates of aggregation were also slower at lower protein concentrations (0.2 mg/ml), but apoE4 still mostly formed higher mass aggregates within 4 h of incubation (Figure 1d).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (faster formation of high-molecular-mass apoE aggregates at lower protein concentration)
rows.Experimental system: Purified, lipid-free recombinant human apoE expressed in E. coli; isolated low-mass apoE at 0.2 mg/ml in 100 mM NH4HCO3, pH 7.8; incubation at 37 °C followed by analytical gel filtration. Comparable behavior was reported in PBS and TBS at pH 7.4. No cells or endo-lysosomal compartments were examined.

rows.Finding description: After overnight preincubation at 37 °C and 0.3 mg/ml, approximately 90% of apoE4 and 10% of apoE3 had aggregated.
rows.Finding quote: Preincubation of tetrameric apoE (0.3 mg/ml) overnight at 37 oC resulted in the aggregation of about 5% of apoE2, 10% of apoE3 and 90% of apoE4.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (higher fraction of apoE aggregated after overnight preincubation)
rows.Experimental system: Purified, lipid-free recombinant human apoE expressed in E. coli; tetrameric preparations at 0.3 mg/ml preincubated overnight at 37 °C before neuronal toxicity experiments. The specific assay used to determine these aggregation percentages and the preincubation buffer are not identified in this sentence. These are preparation measurements, not intracellular measurements in Neuro-2a cells.
rows.Data location: Results, toxicity section, MTT paragraph (preincubated preparations used in Fig 6d)

rows.Finding description: Native PAGE supported greater aggregation of lipid-free recombinant human ApoE4 than ApoE3; data represent two independently prepared ApoE isoform samples.
rows.Finding quote: Together, these results suggest that lipid‐free ApoE has the tendency to aggregate in solution at a concentration of 0.1 mg·mL−1, whereas lipidation is capable of impeding this behavior. This tendency is isoform dependent, with the most pronounced aggregation for ApoE4, followed by ApoE3 and ApoE2 (Fig. 3).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (greater lipid-free apoE aggregation in vitro)
rows.Experimental system: Commercial recombinant human ApoE3 and ApoE4 from Leinco Technologies, lipid-free at 0.1 mg·mL−1 in PBS; native 4–20% Tris-glycine PAGE, with 3 μg ApoE loaded and electrophoresis at 4 °C for 16 h. Cell-free; no endo-lysosomal localization or acidic-pH condition.

rows.Finding description: FFF refractive-index profiles contributed to the authors' conclusion that lipid-free recombinant human ApoE4 self-assembled more than ApoE3; profiles represent two independently prepared ApoE isoform samples.
rows.Finding quote: Our results show that lipid‐free ApoE has the tendency to self‐assemble, with ApoE4 having the highest aggregation propensity, followed by ApoE3 and ApoE2 (Figs 2, 3, 4).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (greater lipid-free apoE self-assembly in vitro)
rows.Experimental system: Commercial recombinant human ApoE3 and ApoE4 from Leinco Technologies, lipid-free at 0.1 mg·mL−1 in PBS; asymmetrical flow field flow fractionation with differential refractive-index detection. Cell-free, without endosomes or lysosomes; no acidic-pH experiment or aggregation time course reported.
rows.Data location: Fig 2A; Discussion sentence attributing the isoform-dependent self-assembly ranking to Figs 2, 3, 4

rows.Finding description: After purification, apoE4M lacking residues 1–23 aggregated almost instantaneously, whereas the corresponding apoE3M construct required several hours.
rows.Finding quote: Interestingly, while the aggregation of ApoE4M-AP occurred almost instantaneously, it took several hours to observe the aggregation of ApoE3M-AP.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3M-AP -> apoE4M-AP) -> (faster apoE aggregation)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3M and apoE4M, each carrying F257A/W264R/V269A/L279Q/V287E and deletion of residues 1–23. Aggregation observed following size-exclusion purification. This is an engineered, lipid-free protein system without endo-lysosomes.
rows.Data location: Results accompanying Fig. 3G: “Interestingly, while the aggregation of ApoE4M-AP occurred almost instantaneously, it took several hours to observe the aggregation of ApoE3M-AP.”

rows.Finding description: Adding SPA reduced apoE4 aggregation toward the apoE3 level during static light scattering at 37 °C, with three replicates.
rows.Finding quote: The signal from light scattering decreased in the presence of both SPA (Fig. 5A) and tramiprosate (Supplementary Fig. 10), suggesting the reduction of ApoE4 aggregation.
rows.Finding summary: (SPA added to apoE4) -> (reduced apoE aggregation)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human wild-type apoE4 at approximately 10 µM, with 20 mM SPA, a 2000-fold molar excess. Static light scattering at 266 nm over 15 hours in Tris buffer at 37 °C and pH 7.4; apoE3 served as a comparator.

rows.Finding description: Truncated apoE4M aggregated almost instantaneously, while four additional interface alanine substitutions prevented aggregation; the photographed AP/AS comparison was reproduced in at least two independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: Interestingly, while the aggregation of ApoE4M-AP occurred almost instantaneously, it took several hours to observe the aggregation of ApoE3M-AP. Subsequent transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis of these aggregates revealed fibril-like morphology in both cases (Fig. 3H). Conversely, no aggregation was observed for ApoE3M-AS and ApoE4M-AS.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE4M-AP -> apoE4M-AS interface mutations) -> (suppressed apoE aggregation)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant ApoE3M and ApoE4M truncation constructs (residues 1-23 deleted); AS variants carry R38A/E45A/E49A/R145A. The Results identify both isoforms for the AP aggregation and AS suppression observations; the Fig. 3G photo is labelled ApoE4M-AS (left) and ApoE4M-AP (right), two hours after purification.

rows.Finding description: Transmission electron microscopy found fibril-like apoE aggregates in both truncated apoE3M and apoE4M preparations, without reporting a quantitative between-isoform difference in fibril burden.
rows.Finding quote: Subsequent transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis of these aggregates revealed fibril-like morphology in both cases (Fig. 3H).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3M-AP -> apoE4M-AP) -> (fibril-like aggregates present in both)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3M-AP and apoE4M-AP, carrying five monomerizing substitutions and deletion of residues 1–23. Negative-stain TEM using approximately 0.4 mg/ml protein and 2% ammonium molybdate. Legend specifically identifies the pictured apoE3M-AP fibrils; Results reports both isoforms.

rows.Finding description: Adaptive simulations showed apoE3 dimer dissociation after approximately 2.5 µs of cumulative sampling, whereas apoE4 did not dissociate even after approximately 10 µs.
rows.Finding quote: While the ApoE3 dimeric unit dissociated after ~ 2.5 µs, the dissociation of the ApoE4 dimeric unit did not occur even after ~ 10 µs.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (greater simulated persistence of the N-terminal dimer)
rows.Experimental system: Adaptive molecular dynamics of human apoE N-terminal dimers initialized from apoE3 structure 1BZ4 and apoE4 structure 8AX9. Simulations used 310 K, pH 7.4 protonation and 0.1 M salt. Reported times are cumulative adaptive sampling, not measured cellular lifetimes.

rows.Finding description: The simulated apoE4 dimer had a more favorable mean electrostatic interaction energy, −396 kcal/mol, than apoE3, −338 kcal/mol, a 1.17-fold greater magnitude.
