rows.Finding quote: We also found significantly stronger binding energy in the dimeric unit of ApoE4 than in ApoE3, explaining its resilience to dissociation. These interactions were formed primarily by electrostatic contacts (Supplementary Tables 8 and Supplementary Note 1).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (stronger simulated electrostatic dimer association)
rows.Experimental system: Human apoE N-terminal dimer adaptive molecular dynamics without SPA. Linear interaction energies calculated over the first 500 ns of concatenated trajectories while dimers remained associated; 310 K, pH 7.4 protonation and 0.1 M salt.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Table 8, ApoE3 and ApoE4 Eelec rows

rows.Finding description: Proteolytic mapping lacked N-terminal peptides around residues 31–50 for wild-type apoE3 and 44–52 for wild-type apoE4, indicating interface protection in both with different coverage boundaries.
rows.Finding quote: Based on LC-MS/MS bottom-up proteomics analysis of both ApoEWT and ApoEM, we found that wild-type ApoE3 and ApoE4 isoforms lack peptides in NTD corresponding to residues ~ 31–50 and 44–52, respectively (Fig. 4A, CTD in Supplementary Fig. 7).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3WT -> apoE4WT) -> (different protease-inaccessible regions at the self-association interface)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human wild-type apoE3 and apoE4, compared with monomerizing-mutant proteins, using proteolysis and LC-MS/MS peptide mapping. Missing coverage was interpreted as protection in oligomeric protein, without direct aggregate quantification or endo-lysosomal localization.

rows.Finding description: Simulations showed partial unfolding at H3 residues 89–94 in apoE3 but not apoE4, whereas apoE4 lost helical content at residues 120–124 near Q123.
rows.Finding quote: The results showed partial unfolding at the N-terminus of the H3 helix (residues 89–94) in the case of ApoE3, while no change was observed in ApoE4. Conversely, we observed a significant decrease in α-helical content at the end of the H3 helix (residues 120–124) in ApoE4.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3M -> apoE4M) -> (less N-terminal but greater C-terminal H3 unfolding)
rows.Experimental system: Adaptive simulations of full-length human apoE3M and apoE4M, twenty microseconds cumulative sampling per system at 310 K. Residue-level helical content calculated using DSSP. Misfolding-related structural readout, without endo-lysosomal localization.

rows.Finding description: Crystal-structure analysis found T-shaped packing in 6 of 8 apoE3 structures and V-shaped packing in 5 of 7 apoE4 structures, supporting an isoform-associated difference in self-association geometry.
rows.Finding quote: A comparison of previously solved ApoE structures revealed that ApoE2 and ApoE3 prefer T-shaped packing, as 2 out of 2 ApoE2 structures and 6 out of 8 ApoE3 structures display T-shaped packing. On the other hand, 5 of the 7 ApoE4 structures have V-shaped packing, indicating an ApoE4 preference for this packing pattern.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (greater preference for V-shaped N-terminal self-association)
rows.Experimental system: Comparative crystallographic analysis of human apoE N-terminal domains, combining existing structures with four newly determined apoE4 structures. New crystals arose from recombinant MBP-apoE4M preparations but resolved approximately residues 22–165. Crystal packing is a proposed aggregation surrogate; no brain cells, acidic compartment or endo-lysosomal localization was tested.

rows.Finding description: The apoE4-preferred V-shaped dimer had an approximately 75° interchain angle, compared with approximately 100° for the apoE3-preferred T-shaped dimer, a 25° difference.
rows.Finding quote: While the angle between chains A and B in the T-shaped dimeric unit was ~ 100°, the corresponding angle in the V-shaped dimeric unit was significantly smaller ~ 75°. This ~ 25° angle difference between T-shaped and V-shaped packing was retained in both the orthorhombic and trigonal space groups.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (smaller angle between self-associating N-terminal domains)
rows.Experimental system: Human apoE N-terminal crystal structures; interchain angles derived from principal axes of inertia. Comparison concerns crystal-associated dimers, without cellular or endo-lysosomal aggregation measurements.

rows.Finding description: Compared with apoE3-like T-shaped structures, apoE4 C112R structures formed an R112–E109 salt bridge, lost the R61–E109 interaction and repositioned Q123 toward the proposed aggregation-prone geometry.
rows.Finding quote: The C112R substitution in ApoE4 (Fig. 1C and Supplementary Fig. 2) led to the formation of a new salt bridge between R112 and E109 and the repositioning of R61. Consequently, the helix H2-H3 interaction between R61 and E109 observed in the T-shaped packing was abolished, and the four-helix bundle was destabilized. The “domino-like” effect of the C112R mutation was further exacerbated through the H3 helix up towards Q123, which directly influenced a tilt between chains A and B. The side-chain of Q123 was oriented upwards in the T-shaped packing, while it was rotated downwards in the V-shaped packing.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 C112 -> apoE4 R112) -> (altered intradomain contacts and destabilized four-helix bundle)
rows.Experimental system: Comparative analysis of recombinant human apoE N-terminal crystal structures. The proposed domino mechanism links local structural differences to self-association; aggregation inside cells was not measured.

rows.Finding description: ApoE4 and apoE3 retained the same principal self-association interface, but apoE4 gained a D153–Q46 interaction and displayed a different W34 orientation.
rows.Finding quote: Despite a different tilt in T-shaped and V-shaped dimeric units, the main self-association interface formed by chains A and B remained the same in all ApoE isoforms (Fig. 1D). The key interacting residues that held the two chains together were R38 (H1) and R145 (H4) from chain A and E45 and E49 located in helix 1’ (H1’) of chain B. Additionally, a new specific interaction in ApoE4 was formed between D153 from chain A and Q46 from chain B as both chains were tilted in the ApoE4 structure. Moreover, E45 which interacts with R38 and R145, moved to the center of the “self-association interface”, causing a re-orientation of the W34 side chain upwards.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (additional contact within a shared self-association interface)
rows.Experimental system: Human apoE N-terminal crystal dimers, comparing apoE3-preferred T-shaped and apoE4-preferred V-shaped interfaces. No cellular compartment or aggregation amount was measured.

rows.Finding description: Wild-type apoE4 and apoE3 showed different hydrogen-deuterium uptake around residue 112 and in H3, H4 and the C-terminal domain, indicating isoform-dependent conformation and solvent accessibility.
rows.Finding quote: The main differences between wild-type ApoE3 and ApoE4 isoforms in HDX-MS analysis were the deuterium uptakes (Fig. 4B and Supplementary Fig. 8) observed around position 112, including helix H3 (residues 79–123) and helix H4 (residues 134–136). Moreover, some differences were observed for the CTD, suggesting that C112R substitution has a long-range impact on the entire ApoE molecule and its tetramerization.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3WT -> apoE4WT) -> (altered solvent accessibility in aggregation-associated protein regions)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human wild-type apoE3 and apoE4; HDX-MS at room temperature in Tris/NaCl buffer, D2O buffer pHread 7.1. Exchange measured at 60, 120 and 600 seconds; main figure shows 60 seconds. No cellular or endo-lysosomal assay.

rows.Finding description: Simulated apoE4M H3 was approximately 7° less straight than apoE3M H3 and had a broader, skewed bending-angle distribution.
rows.Finding quote: We found that the H3 helix was ~ 7° straighter in ApoE3M than in ApoE4M. Moreover, ApoE4M showed a more spread and skewed distribution.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3M -> apoE4M) -> (increased H3 bending)
rows.Experimental system: Full-length human apoE3M and apoE4M adaptive molecular dynamics, twenty microseconds cumulative sampling per system at 310 K. H3 bending measured using the Cα atoms of residues 95, 106 and 117, with 180° representing an unbent helix. No cells or aggregates measured.

rows.Finding description: Both apoE3M and apoE4M were characterized as monomerized, rather than showing greater apoE4 oligomerization; no statistical between-isoform difference was reported.
rows.Finding quote: Moreover, we observed that the five mutations previously introduced into the ApoE code to monomerize both isoforms (ApoEM) simultaneously inhibit their aggregation (Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3M -> apoE4M) -> (shared monomerized state)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3M and apoE4M carrying F257A/W264R/V269A/L279Q/V287E. Sedimentation velocity analytical ultracentrifugation at 0.8 mg/ml, 20 °C and 50,000 rpm, analyzed by continuous c(s) distributions. The supplied figure image is unavailable.

rows.Finding description: The simulated apoE4 dimer had mean van der Waals interaction energy of −41 kcal/mol versus −37 kcal/mol for apoE3, a 1.11-fold greater magnitude.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (slightly stronger simulated van der Waals dimer association)
rows.Experimental system: Human apoE N-terminal dimers without SPA; linear interaction energies from the first 500 ns of associated, concatenated adaptive MD trajectories at 310 K and pH 7.4 protonation.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Table 8, ApoE3 and ApoE4 EvdW rows

rows.Finding description: With SPA, the simulated apoE4 dimer retained a more favorable mean electrostatic interaction energy, −322 kcal/mol, than apoE3, −250 kcal/mol, a 1.29-fold greater magnitude.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE3+ SPA Eelec = -250 ± 69 EvdW = -39 ± 7 R145, R38, R142, R32, D35 E49, E45, E50 ApoE4+ SPA Eelec = -322 ± 73
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 + SPA -> apoE4 + SPA) -> (stronger simulated electrostatic dimer association)
rows.Experimental system: Human apoE N-terminal dimer adaptive MD with SPA; energies computed during the first 500 ns of concatenated associated trajectories. Simulations at 310 K, pH 7.4 protonation and 0.1 M salt.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Table 8, ApoE3+SPA and ApoE4+SPA Eelec rows

rows.Finding description: In simulations, the dominant W34 side-chain population was around χ1 = 180° in apoE3M and around χ1 = 300° in apoE4M.
rows.Finding quote: We found that ApoE3M displayed a majority of its population around χ1 = 180° while ApoE4M was mostly around χ1 = 300°.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3M -> apoE4M) -> (different W34 conformation at the self-association interface)
rows.Experimental system: Adaptive molecular dynamics of full-length human apoE3M and homology-modeled apoE4M, with five C-terminal monomerizing mutations. Twenty microseconds cumulative sampling per system at 310 K and pH 7.4 protonation; W34 χ1 distributions measured. Structural surrogate, not an aggregate measurement.

rows.Finding description: Across three cultures, ApoE puncta size showed no significant difference across ApoE3/ApoE4 and vehicle/bafilomycin conditions, whose means were 10.3, 9.0, 9.6, and 9.4 pixels, respectively.
rows.Finding quote: No significant difference in ApoE puncta size was observed after Baf A1 treatment in ApoE3- and ApoE4-treated neurons (mean ApoE puncta size: ApoE3 + DMSO: 10.3 pixels, ApoE3 + Baf A1: 9.0 pixels, ApoE4 + DMSO: 9.6 pixels, and ApoE4 + Baf A1: 9.4 pixels) (Kruskal–Wallis test, P = 0.7064); number of cultures: 3; number of neurons analyzed within each culture: 6–7; for each neuron, 10 neurites were analyzed and averaged.
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4, with or without lysosomal inhibition) -> (no change in neuritic ApoE puncta size)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical/hippocampal cultures from embryonic ApoE-knockout mice at DIV19; conditioned media from primary human APOE3- or APOE4-targeted-replacement mouse astrocytes for four hours, following one-hour pretreatment with 10 nM bafilomycin A1 or DMSO. ApoE puncta size measured in neuritic regions by Fiji particle analysis. Three cultures, six to seven neurons per culture, ten neurites averaged per neuron.

rows.Finding description: In three cultures receiving ApoE4, bafilomycin reduced median ApoE–LAMP1 overlap from 8.7% to 6.3%, with no significant difference.
rows.Finding quote: The percentages of ApoE co-localizing to LAMP1-positive pixels increased from 5.2–9.8% (Mann–Whitney test, P = 0.0864) in ApoE3-treated and decreased from 8.7–6.3% (Mann–Whitney test, P = 0.4358) in ApoE4-treated neurons after Baf A1 treatment (compared with DMSO control), although these changes were not statistically significant; number of cultures: 3; number of neurons analyzed within each culture: 7; for each neuron, 10 neurites were analyzed and averaged.
rows.Finding summary: (lysosomal acidification inhibition in ApoE4-treated neurons) -> (no change in ApoE–LAMP1 overlap)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical/hippocampal cultures from embryonic ApoE-knockout mice at DIV19; 10 nM bafilomycin A1 or DMSO for one hour before four-hour co-treatment with conditioned medium from human APOE4-targeted-replacement mouse astrocytes. Neuritic ApoE–LAMP1 pixel overlap measured by epifluorescence imaging and Fiji. Three cultures, seven neurons per culture, ten neurites averaged per neuron.

rows.Finding description: In the experiment using three cultures per isoform, ApoE3 and ApoE4 showed no significant difference in LAMP1 overlap, a localization surrogate for lysosomal ApoE accumulation.
rows.Finding quote: However, there was no statistically significant difference in ApoE and LAMP1 co-localization between ApoE3 and ApoE4 (Figs 1G and I, P = 0.2744).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (no change in ApoE–LAMP1 pixel overlap)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse N2a cells treated with 2.5 μg/ml recombinant human ApoE3 or ApoE4 for four hours; representative epifluorescence images stained for ApoE and LAMP1. Corresponding pixel-overlap quantification in Fig 1I used three cultures per isoform and five cells per culture. LAMP1 does not uniquely identify lysosomes.

rows.Finding description: In the experiment using three cultures per isoform, ApoE3 and ApoE4 showed no significant difference in Rab7 overlap, a surrogate for late-endosomal ApoE localization.
rows.Finding quote: In comparison with LAMP1, a lower proportion of human ApoE puncta co-localized with Rab7 in N2a cells after 4 h, although there was no significant difference between ApoE3 compared with ApoE4 (Figs 1H and J; P = 0.3392).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (no change in ApoE–Rab7 pixel overlap)
rows.Experimental system: Mouse N2a cells treated with 2.5 μg/ml recombinant human ApoE3 or ApoE4 for four hours; representative ApoE and Rab7 epifluorescence images. Corresponding quantification in Fig 1J used three cultures per isoform and five cells per culture. Rab7 also occurs in autophagic compartments.

rows.Finding description: Cortical fractionation in mice at 3 and 22 months, with 4–6 mice/genotype, showed an increased insoluble-to-soluble apoE ratio with aging in APOE4 mice and a smaller upward trend in APOE3 mice, without identifying the aggregates' cellular compartment.
rows.Finding quote: Intriguingly, the level of insoluble apoE was significantly increased in aged apoE4-TR mice compared with that in young mice (Figure 7E), leading to an increased insoluble to soluble ratio of apoE with aging (Figure 7F). To a lesser extent, there was a trend of an increased insoluble to soluble apoE ratio with aging in apoE3-TR mice (Figures 7E, F).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (more pronounced age-associated increase in the cortical insoluble-to-soluble apoE ratio)
rows.Experimental system: Human APOE3- or APOE4-targeted-replacement mice, with the endogenous murine Apoe locus replaced by human APOE; mixed sexes, 3 and 22 months old; cortical RIPA-soluble and guanidine-extracted detergent-insoluble apoE quantified by ELISA and used to calculate the insoluble-to-soluble ratio; no AD model or endosome/lysosome localization reported.

rows.Finding description: Scanning electron microscopy showed more evident fibrillar-like surface aggregates after apoE4 than apoE3 treatment in differentiated SH-SY5Y cells and SDC3 transfectants, especially at 18 h, across three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: Electron microscopic studies also show the formation of fibrillar-like aggregates on the surfaces of ApoE4-treated cells, especially at 18 h of incubation. The presence of such small fibrils on ApoE3-treated cells was less evident, while electron microscopy did not reveal ApoE2 fibrils on ApoE2-treated SH-SY5Y cells and SDC3 transfectants (Figure 5D).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (more evident fibrillar-like apoE aggregates on cell surfaces)
rows.Experimental system: Human SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells, differentiated WT cells and stable SDC3-overexpressing derivatives; recombinant apoE3 or apoE4 at 500 nM for 3 or 18 h at 37 °C without added Aβ; scanning electron microscopy of cell surfaces. The reported aggregates were surface-associated, with no endosomal or lysosomal localization.

rows.Finding description: SEC profiling of control brain lysates showed a trend toward more large-sized soluble apoE in APOE4 carriers, but no significant difference from non-carriers was reported for the control comparison.
rows.Finding quote: APOE4 carriers showed a greater amount of larger size APOE protein (fraction #26 to #30) than APOE4 non-carriers, although the difference was not significant due to large sample-to-sample variations (Fig. 5e).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE4 non-carrier -> APOE4 carrier) -> (no change in large-sized soluble apoE reaching statistical significance in control brains)
rows.Experimental system: Human postmortem control superior temporal cortex from the a brain bank Jacksonville brain bank; bulk tissue without identified cell types or endo-lysosomal localization. Control cohort APOE4 non-carriers had median age 82.5 years, range 79–91; carriers had median age 87 years, range 61–97. Ages and exact genotypes of the 4–5 SEC samples per group were not separately specified. TBS-soluble lysates underwent tandem Superose 6 SEC at pH 7.4 and apoE ELISA. Fig. 5d displays size distributions; the reported genotype comparison is summarized in Fig. 5e. ApoE molecular size does not establish endo-lysosomal aggregation.
rows.Data location: Fig. 5d; corresponding control fraction comparisons in Fig. 5e

rows.Finding description: Comparing control brain SEC fractions 26–30 showed no significant difference in large-sized soluble apoE between APOE4 carriers and non-carriers despite a higher trend in carriers, with 4–5 samples per group.
rows.Finding quote: APOE4 carriers showed a greater amount of larger size APOE protein (fraction #26 to #30) than APOE4 non-carriers, although the difference was not significant due to large sample-to-sample variations (Fig. 5e).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE4 non-carrier -> APOE4 carrier) -> (no change in large-sized soluble apoE reaching statistical significance in control brain fractions 26–30)
rows.Experimental system: Human postmortem control superior temporal cortex from the a brain bank Jacksonville brain bank; bulk tissue with no specified cell type or organelle localization. Control cohort APOE4 non-carriers had median age 82.5 years, range 79–91; carriers had median age 87 years, range 61–97. Exact ages and genotypes of the 4–5 SEC samples per group were not separately reported. TBS-soluble lysates underwent tandem Superose 6 SEC at pH 7.4, followed by apoE ELISA and Student t tests. Larger apoE-containing species were measured without demonstrating apoE homo-oligomers or endo-lysosomal aggregates.

rows.Finding description: SEC followed by apoE ELISA showed more large-sized soluble apoE in fractions 27–29 in AD brains without LB pathology from APOE4 carriers than non-carriers, using six pooled samples per group.
rows.Finding quote: In AD cases without LB pathology, APOE4 carriers had more large-sized APOE (fractions #27-#29) compared to APOE4 non-carriers (Fig. 5a–c).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE4 non-carrier -> APOE4 carrier) -> (more large-sized soluble apoE in AD brains without LB pathology)
rows.Experimental system: Human postmortem superior temporal cortex from autopsy-confirmed AD cases without LB pathology, a brain bank Jacksonville brain bank; bulk tissue, with no cell-type or endo-lysosomal localization. APOE4 non-carriers included APOE2/3 and APOE3/3; carriers included APOE2/4, APOE3/4, and APOE4/4. Respective cohort age medians were 81 and 83 years, with ranges 55–96 and 55–100; SEC-subset ages were not separately reported. Six samples per group, each pooling equal amounts of TBS lysate from 3–4 brains. Tandem Superose 6 SEC at pH 7.4 followed by apoE ELISA measured molecular-size distributions, without establishing whether larger species were apoE homo-oligomers or other apoE-containing complexes.
rows.Data location: Fig 5b, fractions 27-29 (AD E4- vs AD E4+); size profiles in Fig 5a

rows.Finding description: Reducing SDS-PAGE of preparations containing ApoE3 or ApoE4 showed approximately 70-kDa bands assigned to ApoE dimers, including ApoE-only aggregate controls, without reporting whether dimer abundance differed between isoforms.
rows.Finding quote: We observed also some higher molecular weight bands of ~70 kDa in SDS-PAGE lanes, as shown in Figure 4A, corresponding to S100A9 aggregated with ApoE isoforms. These bands correspond to the dimer of ApoE as they appeared in the lanes, which contain only ApoE aggregates (Figure 4A).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (relative ApoE dimer abundance unresolved; ApoE dimers reported in the isoform experiment)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free recombinant human ApoE3 and ApoE4 preparations, with lipid-free and DOPC/cholesterol-lipidated samples included. Fig 4A examines samples after 70 h at 42 °C in PBS using reducing SDS-PAGE and Coomassie staining; co-incubation samples contained 50 μM S100A9 and 2 μM ApoE. ApoE-only controls were also loaded. The text does not resolve the dimer signal by every lipidation/isoform lane.

rows.Finding description: In recombinant-protein experiments performed three times, PUFA-phospholipid incubation induced disulfide-linked ApoE3 dimerization but had no apparent effect on ApoE4 dimerization, opposing increased ApoE4 oligomerization under these cell-free conditions.
rows.Finding quote: Incubation with the PUFA-phospholipid PE-18:0/22:4n-6 had no apparent effect on ApoE4 dimerization (A). By contrast, incubation of ApoE3 (B) and ApoE2 (C) with PE-18:0/22:4n-6 produced prominent peaks with molecular weights corresponding to ApoE dimers and multimers, respectively.
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (less PUFA-phospholipid-induced disulfide-linked apoE dimerization)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free recombinant human ApoE3 and ApoE4 incubated with PE-18:0/22:4n-6; protein separation and anti-ApoE immunodetection using the Jess automated capillary nano-immunoassay with chemiluminescence. DTT reversal supported disulfide dependence. Incubation duration and pH were not supplied; no brain cells or endosomal/lysosomal localization were examined.

rows.Finding description: Across three LysoIP replicates, human-APOE4-expressing murine Neuro-2a cells showed greater lysosomal APOE abundance than human-APOE3-expressing cells, providing an accumulation surrogate without measuring apoE aggregation.
rows.Finding quote: Through this approach, we found that HsAPOE4-expressing lysosomes accumulated APOE itself, AD-associated secretase proteins (PSEN2, CD63, TSPAN3), trafficking receptors (AP1S1, AP1G1, BET1L, LAMTOR1, LAMTOR2, TMED5), and lipid/glycan-regulators (ACSL4, ACBD3, GALNT2, MAN2B1, NEU1, PIP4P1, SACM1L, PIP4P1/TMEM55B, UXS1) (Figure 3B,C, Figure S3C).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher lysosomal APOE abundance)
rows.Experimental system: Male murine Neuro-2a neuroblastoma cells carrying transgenic full-length human APOE3 or APOE4; endogenous mouse Apoe intact; passages 5–10; TMEM192-3xHA LysoIP in biological and technical triplicates followed by quantitative DIA mass spectrometry with normalization to the TMEM192 lysosomal tag; whether the genotype comparison used untreated LysoIPs only is not stated (BafA1-treated and untreated LysoIPs were both collected).

rows.Finding description: Native-PAGE of non-AD human control CSF showed a lower apoE dimer/monomer ratio in APOE ε3/ε4 than ε3/ε3 samples (ratio D/M 0.38 versus 2.20, printed in the text).
rows.Finding quote: In the control group, the dimer/monomer quotient was significantly lower in the APOE ε3/ε4 group (ratio D/M = 0.38) compared to that of the ε3/ε3 group (ratio D/M = 2.20; p= 0.006), associated to the inability of the apoE4 isoform to form disulfide-linked dimers.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE ε3/ε3 -> APOE ε3/ε4) -> (lower CSF apoE dimer/monomer ratio)
rows.Experimental system: Human non-AD Gothenburg control lumbar CSF; APOE ε3/ε3 versus ε3/ε4; corresponding cohort mean ages 69±2 and 62±5 years; unheated native-PAGE and AB178479 immunoblotting. Bands were assigned as monomers and dimers using denatured CSF and recombinant apoE3 references. No cellular or endo-lysosomal localization was measured.
rows.Data location: Fig. 3D quantification; Fig. 3C representative native blots; Supplementary p. 7 complete source blots

rows.Finding description: Native-PAGE of human AD CSF showed a lower apoE dimer/monomer ratio in APOE ε4/ε4 than ε3/ε3 samples (ratio D/M 0.24 versus 2.27, printed in the text); the Fig. 3D bracket between these groups reads p < 0.0001.
rows.Finding quote: The same situation was found in the AD group, where the dimer/monomer ratio decreased as the ε4 allele was present (ε3/ε3: ratio D/M = 2.27; ε3/ε4: ratio D/M = 1.04; ε4/ε4: ratio D/M = 0.24).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE ε3/ε3 -> APOE ε4/ε4) -> (lower CSF apoE dimer/monomer ratio in AD)
rows.Experimental system: Human Gothenburg AD lumbar CSF, APOE ε3/ε3 versus ε4/ε4; corresponding cohort mean ages 79±2 and 73±1 years; unheated native-PAGE and AB178479 immunoblotting. Extracellular native apoE complexes were measured, without cell-type or compartment identification.
rows.Data location: Fig. 3D quantification; Fig. 3C representative native blots; Supplementary p. 7 complete source blots

rows.Finding description: Reducing SDS-PAGE of Gothenburg AD CSF showed significantly less approximately 100-kDa apoE-containing complex immunoreactivity in APOE ε4/ε4 than ε3/ε3 patients, with 15 patients per genotype.
rows.Finding quote: In the AD group, the 100-kDa apoE species levels were significantly lower in the APOE ε4/ε4 group when compared to both ε3/ε3 (p < 0.0001) and ε3/ε4 (p < 0.0001) groups.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE ε3/ε3 -> APOE ε4/ε4) -> (lower reducing-agent-resistant ~100-kDa CSF apoE complex abundance in AD)
rows.Experimental system: Human Gothenburg AD lumbar CSF, APOE ε3/ε3 versus ε4/ε4; 15 patients per genotype, mean ages 79±2 and 73±1 years; samples heated at 98°C for 5 minutes and analyzed by reducing SDS-PAGE and AB178479 immunoblotting, normalized to recombinant apoE3. No intracellular localization was measured.
rows.Data location: Fig. 4I quantification; Fig. 4A representative blot; Supplementary p. 8 complete source blots

rows.Finding description: Reducing SDS-PAGE of Barcelona AD CSF showed significantly less approximately 100-kDa apoE-containing complex immunoreactivity in nine APOE ε4/ε4 patients than in ten ε3/ε3 patients. Group values printed on the figure: Panel I printed medians: ε3/ε3 3.7 and ε4/ε4 2.8; approximately 24% lower in ε4/ε4; bracket p = 0.02.
rows.Finding quote: Within the AD group, the APOE ε4/ε4 samples once again displayed significantly lower 100-kDa apoE levels compared with ε3/ε3 cases (p = 0.02).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE ε3/ε3 -> APOE ε4/ε4) -> (lower reducing-agent-resistant ~100-kDa CSF apoE complex abundance in AD)
rows.Experimental system: Human Barcelona SPIN cohort AD lumbar CSF, APOE ε3/ε3 versus ε4/ε4; ten and nine patients, respectively, mean ages 75±2 and 72±2 years; heated reducing SDS-PAGE and AB178479 immunoblotting, normalized to recombinant apoE3. No intracellular localization was measured.
rows.Data location: Fig. 5I quantification; Fig. 5A representative blot; Supplementary p. 9 complete source blot

rows.Finding description: Across the sampled ages, APPPS1:E4 and APPPS1:E3 mice showed no significant genotype main effect on apoE levels in the insoluble, guanidine-extracted whole-hemibrain fraction.
rows.Finding quote: We measured apolipoprotein levels in the guanidine hydrochloride-soluble brain fractions. APPPS1:E4 mice exhibited a main effect of age (p = 0.0003), with 16-month-old mice displaying significantly higher levels of apoE than the two younger age groups (Figure 4S). There was no main effect of the APOE allele when evaluating both the APPPS1:E3 and APPPS1:E4 mice (Figure 4T, p = 0.2003).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (no change in insoluble whole-hemibrain apoE levels)
rows.Experimental system: Whole hemibrains from eight-, 12-, and 16-month-old APPswe/PS1dE9 heterozygous mice homozygous for human APOE3 or APOE4 targeted replacement, C57BL/6 background; sexes pooled; Tper-insoluble material extracted with guanidine hydrochloride and apoE measured using HJ15.6 capture and HJ15.4b detection antibodies; 3-11 mice/group; no subcellular localization.
rows.Data location: Fig 4T, genotype main effect across ages

rows.Finding description: At 12 months, insoluble whole-hemibrain apoE levels appeared higher in APPPS1:E4 mice than APPPS1:E3 mice, but there was no significant difference.
rows.Finding quote: Mice with the APOE4 allele appeared to have higher apoE levels at 12 and 16 months, but the difference was insignificant.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (no change in insoluble whole-hemibrain apoE levels at 12 months)
rows.Experimental system: Whole hemibrains from 12-month-old APPswe/PS1dE9 heterozygous mice homozygous for human APOE3 or APOE4 targeted replacement, C57BL/6 background; sexes pooled; Tper-insoluble material extracted with guanidine hydrochloride and apoE measured using HJ15.6 capture and HJ15.4b detection antibodies; legend reports 3-11 mice/group across this panel; no subcellular localization.

rows.Finding description: At 300–310 K, 11.12% of simulated ApoE4 conformations versus 0.05% of ApoE3 conformations met the authors' intermediate-similarity criterion.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE Isoform Population of Intermediate from 300 to 310 K E2 70.66 % E3 0.05 % E4 11.12 %
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (higher simulated intermediate-like conformational population at 300–310 K)
rows.Experimental system: Human full-length apoE monomers in implicit-solvent REX/DMD; conformations at 300–310 K classified against each isoform's own T3 intermediate centroid using N-terminal helical RMSD less than 15 Å; no human brain cells, endo-lysosomes, or intermolecular aggregation.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Table 4, E3 and E4 rows

rows.Finding description: The summary table reports intermediate-like populations of 11.1% for ApoE4 versus 0.1% for ApoE3 at 300–310 K, using rounded values from Supplementary Table 4.
rows.Finding quote: Population of intermediate state at 300 to 310 K 70.7 % 0.1 % 11.1 %
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (higher simulated intermediate-like population at 300–310 K)
rows.Experimental system: Human full-length apoE monomer REX/DMD; intermediate-like conformations defined by N-terminal helical RMSD less than 15 Å from each isoform's own intermediate centroid; rounded summary of Supplementary Table 4, not independent evidence.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Table 7, Population of intermediate state at 300 to 310 K row

rows.Finding description: Intermediate-state clustering showed two separating helix pairs in ApoE3 but separation of helix–1 alone in ApoE4, which the authors identified as a unique misfolded intermediate.
rows.Finding quote: Specifically, we observe a decrease in the hydrophobic contacts of ApoE2’s N-terminal domain helices (Fig 3B) and ApoE3’s N-terminal domain separating into two helix pairs (Fig 3C). More importantly, we identify a unique intermediate state for ApoE4 (Discussion section), in which only helix–1 separates from the N-terminal domain helix bundle (Fig 3D).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (isoform-specific simulated misfolded intermediate with separated helix–1)
rows.Experimental system: Human full-length apoE monomers in implicit-solvent REX/DMD; centroid structures of the most populated N-terminal RMSD clusters from PMF basins; ApoE3 at 338 K and ApoE4 at 328 K; no apoE oligomers or cellular compartments modeled.

rows.Finding description: At their respective intermediate temperatures, simulated ApoE4 occupied a distinct, more compact conformational landscape than ApoE3, consistent with an isoform-specific misfolded monomer.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE3 is characterized by both the native and alternate N-terminal domain conformations, while ApoE2 visits only the latter. ApoE4 exhibits a unique, more compact intermediate conformational state as denoted by the smaller range of RMSD and Rg values compared to the two other variants.
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (distinct, more compact simulated intermediate conformational landscape)
rows.Experimental system: Human full-length apoE monomer models in implicit-solvent REX/DMD; ApoE3 at 338 K versus ApoE4 at 328 K; potential-of-mean-force landscapes using N-terminal helical Cα RMSD and radius of gyration, excluding the flexible C-terminal domain from reaction coordinates; no cellular or endo-lysosomal system.

rows.Finding description: At intermediate temperatures, simulated ApoE3 lacked inter-domain contacts while ApoE4 retained contacts linking residues 26–44, 196–215, and 235–243.
rows.Finding quote: Interestingly, for ApoE4 at temperature T3, we observe a unique series of contacts between residues 26 to 44 in the N-terminal helix–1, residues 196 to 215 in the hinge region, and residues 235 to 243 in the C-terminal domain (Fig 4I outlined in red).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (retained isoform-specific inter-domain contacts in the simulated misfolded intermediate)
rows.Experimental system: Human full-length apoE monomers, implicit-solvent REX/DMD; ApoE3 at 338 K versus ApoE4 at 328 K; pairwise distance analysis of the intermediate ensembles; reported ApoE4 contacts involve N-terminal helix–1, hinge/C-terminal boundary, and C-terminal residues; no measured oligomers or endo-lysosomal localization.
rows.Data location: Fig 4H–I; Results, Inter-domain interactions of ApoE isoforms

rows.Finding description: Among neuronal LRP1-intact APP/PS1 mice at 9 months, APOE4 mice had more GDN-HCl-extractable insoluble hippocampal apoE than APOE3 mice, with 18–23 mice per group.
rows.Finding quote: Insoluble apoE amounts in the GDN-HCl fraction were higher in APP/PS1; APOE4 control mice than in APP/PS1; APOE3 control mice, which was not affected by neuronal LRP1 deficit ( Figure 3I ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4; neuronal LRP1 intact) -> (higher insoluble hippocampal apoE)
rows.Experimental system: Male and female 9-month-old APPswe/PSEN1ΔE9 mice with homozygous human APOE3-targeted replacement or APOE4-targeted replacement, Lrp1 floxed alleles, and no αCaMKII-Cre; hippocampal detergent-insoluble pellet extracted with guanidine hydrochloride and analyzed by protein-normalized apoE ELISA. Tissue insolubility was measured without cell-type or endolysosomal localization; these are amyloid-model mice, not non-aged human cells.

rows.Finding description: Among donors negative for both defined tau pathologies, age- and sex-adjusted analysis found no significant difference in detergent-insoluble cortical apoE between APOE4 and APOE3.
rows.Finding summary: APOE4 versus APOE3 showed no statistically significant difference in insoluble cortical apoE among donors negative for both defined tau pathologies.

Subgroup with Braak stage <4 and no AGD, which does not establish absence of all AD pathology. APOE ε3/ε4 or ε4/ε4 versus ε3/ε3. Formic-acid-solubilized detergent-insoluble apoE ELISA normalized to protein; age/sex-adjusted regression. No organelle localization measured.

rows.Finding description: Age- and sex-adjusted analysis found higher detergent-insoluble apoE in APOE4 than APOE3 temporal cortex, providing an aggregation surrogate without establishing endo-lysosomal localization.
rows.Finding quote: Compared to APOE3, APOE4 was associated with increased levels of insoluble apoE (FA: β = 1.24, p < 0.001) and insoluble pTau181 (FA: β = 0.72, p < 0.001), and decreased detergent-soluble tTau levels (TBSX: β = -0.18, p = 0.002).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher detergent-insoluble cortical apoE)

Frozen temporal cortex, sequential extraction, formic-acid-solubilized detergent-insoluble fraction; apoE sandwich ELISA normalized to total protein. APOE ε3/ε4 or ε4/ε4 versus ε3/ε3; adjusted for age and sex. No cellular or endo-lysosomal localization measured.
rows.Data location: Table 3, APOE4 vs. APOE3, apoE-FA row

rows.Finding description: Descriptively, median detergent-insoluble cortical apoE was higher in 149 APOE4 donors at 128.8 ng/mg protein than in 153 APOE3 donors at 33.7 ng/mg protein.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher median detergent-insoluble cortical apoE)

Formic-acid-solubilized detergent-insoluble apoE measured by sandwich ELISA and normalized to total protein. Unadjusted descriptive medians; no endo-lysosomal localization or aggregate-specific assay.
rows.Data location: Table S3, apoE (ng/mg protein), FA row, APOE3 and APOE4 columns

rows.Finding description: Among AD-tau-negative donors, age- and sex-adjusted analysis found no significant difference in detergent-insoluble cortical apoE between APOE4 carriers and noncarriers.
rows.Finding summary: Among AD-tau-negative donors, the APOE4 carrier–noncarrier difference in insoluble cortical apoE was statistically nonsignificant.

Braak stage <4 subgroup, with and without AGD; absence of defined AD-tau does not establish absence of all AD pathology. APOE4 carriers versus noncarriers including APOE2 and APOE3. Formic-acid-solubilized detergent-insoluble apoE ELISA normalized to protein; age/sex-adjusted regression.
rows.Data location: Table S9, Association with apoE-FA, APOE4 row, No AD-tau pathology column
